title: Car payments, not student loans, are blocking the most first-time buyers
summary: A 2026 survey of 57 lending companies found car payments, not student loans, are now the top reason first-time buyers get denied a mortgage. Here's why, and what to do.
body_text: A recent survey of loan officers at 57 lenders found that car payments, not student loans, are most likely to block a first-time buyer's mortgage approval. Auto loans were cited by 47% of loan officers as the type of debt most commonly stopping an otherwise qualified buyer, compared with 27% for credit card balances and just 15% for student loans. Keep reading for some practical advice about balancing car payments with mortgage approval. The data: what's actually blocking first-time buyers HomeLight's Lender Insights & Predictions for Summer 2026 gathered these findings from loan officers across the country, in a poll fielded between June 10 and June 23, 2026. When asked which type of consumer debt most commonly stops a qualified renter from getting a first mortgage, loan officers pointed to auto loans far more often than any other category. Debt type Share of loan officers who named it as the top blocker Auto loans 47% Credit card balances 27% Student loans 15% One surveyed loan officer in St. Augustine, Fla., with 24 years of experience put it plainly, saying, "There is nothing sexier than a paid-off car." Her broader point: Buyers need a wake-up call about how much a car payment quietly limits their mortgage options. Why car payments hit your mortgage approval harder The reason comes down to how debt-to-income ratio (DTI) works. Lenders add up all of your required monthly debt payments, including your future mortgage payment, and divide that by your gross monthly income. Most lenders cap DTI between 43% and 50%, depending on the loan program. This sounds complex, but ultimately, it's pretty simple: It means any dollar committed to an existing debt is a dollar that can't go toward your mortgage payment. Car loans are particularly costly in this calculation for two reasons. First, they're almost always a fixed, full-amount monthly payment with no minimum-payment flexibility the way credit cards have. A $500 car payment counts as $500 in your DTI every month, with no way to pay less that month if your budget is tight. Second, auto loan terms have stretched out in recent years, meaning many buyers are carrying a larger, longer-term car payment right at the moment they're trying to qualify for a mortgage. Student loans, by comparison, often have income-driven repayment plans or lower monthly obligations relative to the total balance, which can make them lighter on DTI than their headline balance suggests. See your buying power See what you qualify for in as little as 3 minutes — no credit impact How a car payment limits your homebuying power A $300 monthly car payment could reduce the home price range you qualify for by $45,000 to $60,000, depending on your interest rate, loan program, other debts, down payment size, and other variables that are unique to each borrower. Everybody's finances are different, but, for most of us, this is not a rounding error. For a buyer working with a tight budget, a mid-size auto loan can be the difference between qualifying for a starter home and getting denied altogether. This is also why loan officers surveyed said 61% of today's first-time buyers face greater affordability strain than buyers did five years ago, while only 4% said today's buyers are better prepared financially. Rising vehicle prices, and higher financing charges, contribute to this shift. A mortgage calculator can show you how a specific car payment changes the loan amount you'd qualify for, using your actual income and debts rather than a national average. What to do before you apply If you're carrying an auto loan and planning to buy in the next year, a few moves could improve your position: Pay off the car loan first, if you can. Eliminating a car payment has an outsized effect on your DTI compared to chipping away at a larger but lower-payment debt like student loans. Ask about seller-paid closing costs. Rather than saving more cash to bring to closing, some buyers offset costs by negotiating seller credits, which frees up savings for a bigger down payment instead. Loan officers in the same survey named this as the most common money-saving tactic among their first-time buyer clients right now. Don't wait for 20% down. Low-down-payment loans like FHA and Fannie Mae's HomeReady program remain widely used, and 80% of loan officers surveyed said at least 10% of their first-time buyer clients get some financial help from family for their down payment. None of this advice is customized for any specific borrower. To find out exactly how you can best qualify for the mortgage you need, talk to a loan officer or a financial adviser. Frequently asked questions Does a car loan affect my mortgage approval more than student loans? This varies by borrower, but according to a 2026 survey of loan officers, the answer is yes in most cases. Auto loans were named the top blocking debt by 47% of loan officers, compared with 15% for student loans, largely because car payments are fixed and don't have the lower minimum-payment options that many student loan repayment plans offer. Should I pay off my car before applying for a mortgage? If you can pay it off or pay it down significantly without draining your down payment savings, it's often one of the more effective ways to improve your debt-to-income ratio. Talk to a loan officer about your specific numbers before deciding, since the right move depends on your full financial picture. What debt-to-income ratio do I need to qualify for a mortgage? Most lenders look for a DTI at or below 43%, though some loan programs, including FHA, allow higher ratios for otherwise qualified borrowers. Your specific limit depends on the loan program, your credit score, and your down payment. Is a lower car payment better than paying off the loan faster? For DTI purposes, a lower monthly payment helps you qualify for more mortgage, even if it means paying more interest over the life of the auto loan. If you're planning to buy soon, ask your lender whether refinancing your auto loan to a lower payment makes sense for your timeline. Why is student debt talked about so much if it's not the biggest issue? Student debt affects a huge share of buyers and carries emotional weight because of its size, but the survey suggests its actual monthly DTI impact is often smaller than a car payment's, thanks to income-driven repayment plans and extended terms. What's the fastest way to know if my current debt is blocking me from qualifying? A pre-approval is the most reliable way to see your real numbers, since it accounts for your specific income, debts, and credit profile rather than general guidelines. It's worth doing before you start house hunting, not after. Bottom line If you've been waiting to buy because you assumed your student loans would sink your application, it's worth taking another look at your full financial picture. A 2026 survey data suggests a paid-off or low-payment car may matter more to your approval odds than the size of your student debt. Getting pre-approved is the clearest way to find out where you stand. Individual results vary by lender, loan program, and borrower profile.

title: Best Webflow Alternatives: Cost to Stay, Cost to Leave
summary: Six Webflow alternatives priced at 1, 5 and 20 client sites, with what the code export really carries and what a seat costs the client who inherits the site.
body_text: How we checked these numbers Disclosure: Blink is our product, and we rank it first. Nine of the sixteen results ranking for this term are published by a vendor selling the alternative or an agency selling Webflow services; only two are independent, and one of those is affiliate-monetised. We just said so. Webflow's plan and seat prices were read in a real browser on 18 August 2026 , because webflow.com returns a parse error to automated fetching and help.webflow.com returns HTTP 403. Two other pricing pages — Elementor's and Squarespace's — render client-side and served no figures at all, so those prices are third-party and named as such. Wix's did render on 18 August 2026, so its ladder is first-party. We have run no speed tests and no Lighthouse audits. Every performance figure is someone else's published measurement, attributed by name. And where a vendor's own pages contradict each other, we say so and name both. That happens six times below, and five of the six are ours. What Webflow actually costs, and what it locks Webflow's advertised entry price is not the price of a working business site, because you never buy one thing. Webflow's homepage on 18 August 2026 — a "growth engine" pitched to enterprise teams beside Spotify, TED and Dropbox logos, not to the owner paying per site Blink Axis one is the Site plan, priced per website. Starter is $0 on a webflow.io subdomain with ~2 pages and a lifetime cap of 50 form submissions. Basic is $15/mo billed yearly and has no CMS at all , so any site with a blog starts higher; Premium is $25/mo billed yearly. Axis two is the Workspace plan, priced per team. Starter is free but cannot export code. Core is $19/mo billed yearly with code export, Growth $49/mo, Freelancer $16/mo and Agency $35/mo, all with export. Axis three is seats, priced per person. One Full Seat comes with each Workspace plan; the next is $39/mo billed yearly, a Limited Seat is $15/mo billed yearly, and the Reviewer seat is free but view-and-comment only. Then the escalations arrive without asking. Premium includes 50 GB of bandwidth, down from the old Business plan's 100 GB , as UltimateWB documented — bots and every HTTP status code count toward it, and exceeding it two months running upgrades your plan for you. AI credits landed 13 May 2026, enforced from 29 June at 200/300/400 per month by tier, with no published credits-per-generation rate card. The May 2026 restructure was not uniform. NoCode.Tech quotes an agency owner who audited 14 client sites and found 9 better off, 3 neutral, 2 worse . A coin flip per client, not a price cut. Two capabilities also vanished inside eighteen months. Webflow Logic was disabled 27 June 2025, and User Accounts — native memberships and gated content — was discontinued 29 January 2026 , pushing gated content onto services such as Memberstack from roughly $25/mo. Both dates rest on one source, BRIX Templates. Webflow gives you the most direct visual control of any tool on this page, and nothing here is going to pretend otherwise. Box model, flexbox and breakpoints, exposed and operated by you. It emits clean semantic HTML, Webflow University is free, and its standing is verified: 4.5 out of 5 across 266 reviews on Capterra . None of that is why you are leaving. You are leaving because the bill multiplies with the work, and the way out does not carry a running site. "I do not want an AI to build my website" That fear has a specific author. The most-upvoted leaver thread of 2026 in r/webflow opens with the poster ruling it out unprompted: " if you are here to just recommend Claude Code, please know that I have no interest in using AI tools to build websites " — r/webflow . It is not a silly fear: a generated site you cannot control, cannot restructure, cannot hand to a client. Half of it is right. Where it is right. Independent reviewers describe a real ceiling. One — affiliate-disclosed, and balanced — documented asking Blink to move a logout button to the footer and having the agent delete the footer entirely . A 25-year practitioner reported the agent producing a ~3,000-line backend file that then choked further progress. Credit spend also scales with prompt vagueness rather than task size, the mechanism behind most cost surprises. If you sell design craft, those are the right reasons to stay on a canvas tool. Where it is wrong. "Type a prompt, accept whatever appears" is not the loop. You edit by pointing. The visual editor shipped 6 June 2026: point and click any element and edit it directly, without writing a prompt at all. That is a different mechanic from regenerating a page and hoping. You can read and take the code. Code download is available from Starter up, and two-way GitHub sync means edits you make in VS Code or Cursor pull back into the project. Blink's terms state you "retain full ownership" of what you create, with the right to "use, modify, distribute, publish, sell, or open-source" it. So the honest claim is narrower than "AI replaces the designer", and it is checkable: the first draft arrives built instead of blank, and every change after that is one you make. If you sell design craft, stay on Webflow. If what you sell is a finished site a client can run, this is the whole job. 1. Blink — the bill does not scale with your client count Blink's landing page — the whole interface is one prompt box and four build targets, so the first draft comes from a description rather than a template Blink Price: Free ($0, preview URLs only) · Starter $25/mo, or $150/yr billed annually · Pro $50/mo, or $300/yr · Max from $200/mo, or $1,200/yr at the entry rung · Team $40/seat/mo, or $240/seat/yr billed annually , with a 3-seat minimum , so the real Team floor is $120/month on monthly billing, or $720/yr billed annually. Best for: the agency, the designer and the inheriting owner who want the finished site, not the craft of building it Describe the business and Blink designs and builds the site for it, then hosts it on your custom domain with SSL issued within 5–10 minutes of DNS verification. The 42+ production-ready templates , read on 18 August 2026, span landing pages, portfolios, storefronts and dashboards — and they are optional, because the default path is a site built from your description. The billing shape is the whole argument for an agency. There is no per-site plan and no per-seat wall around your client. Team workspaces pool credits across every seat, make viewer seats unlimited and free , and strand no credit on an inactive member. On Webflow your tenth client site is a tenth Site plan. Changes are direct. Click an element in the visual editor and edit it without writing a prompt, or hand a batch of revisions to the agent in plain English. That is what ends the retainer. The stack is included, not assembled. A dedicated managed SQL database per project with row-level security built in , built-in authentication across six providers with no OAuth apps to configure, plus file storage, queue, real-time and email — none of it a separate subscription. SEO is a panel, not a project. The SEO & AI Search panel shipped 15 June 2026: it scans the live site and controls titles, meta descriptions, sitemap, robots.txt and JSON-LD in-product. The honest limitations, stated plainly. The free tier is a preview, not a live site — production hosting, a custom domain and code download all start at Starter. Starter and Pro credits reset each cycle and do not roll over , hosting traffic draws on the same pool as building, though overages never take your app offline , and all fees are non-refundable. One material unknown for anyone whose traffic pays the bills: neither Blink's SEO page nor its tech-stack page states whether server-side rendering or prerendering is available — we will not infer it on our own behalf. And five places our own pages disagree with each other or with the product , since we are asking you to check everyone else's. Our /faq says every Blink app "includes free hosting with SSL certificates, global CDN, custom domain support", contradicting the Starter+ gate in /docs/faq. Our /docs/faq puts Team at $50/seat with a 2-seat minimum against $40/seat and a 3-seat minimum in the live catalog. And /docs/faq says Max credits roll over while /faq scopes rollover to teams on 800+ credit tiers. Two more are worse than doc drift. The Starter database ceiling is documented at 5 GB and enforced at 2 GB in shipped code. And our docs advertise 90-day point-in-time recovery, while our own disaster-recovery check on 18 August 2026 restored 0 of 5 namespaces — treat that window as unproven until we say otherwise. Verdict: if your problem is that the platform bills you per site and per person and then will not let the client touch it, this is the one. Start free at blink.new , or read Blink vs Webflow . 2. Framer — the design-led successor, if you never need the files Framer's homepage, selling itself as a "design agent" — the shot behind it is a CMS table driving a published page, the part you can never export Blink Price: Free ($0, Framer subdomain, no custom domain) · Basic $10/mo on the yearly toggle ($120/yr) · Pro $30/mo yearly ($360/yr). Editor seats are separate: $20/editor/month , or $10 for a content-only editor. Best for: a designer who lives in a canvas, producing marketing sites Framer is the obvious successor and it deserves the position. Its motion capability is the productized descendant of the Motion library, and the strongest evidence for its design fidelity is adversarial: its harshest 1-star Capterra reviewer opens by crediting the templates. Do not let anyone tell you Framer is weak on SEO. Framer sites are server-rendered React, with the most-visited pages pre-rendered at publish time and the long tail rendered on first request. Crawlers get HTML, and EXPERTE scores Framer 8 out of 8 on SEO features. Framer 3.0 shipped 16 June 2026 with agents working on the canvas itself, and moved pricing in the customer's favour: editor seats cut from $40 to $20, plus a $10 Content Editor role. Three things to price. Seats are a second billing axis, billed monthly even on an annual site plan. On Basic, one extra editor at $240/yr costs more than the $120/yr site plan it sits on, and seats cap at 10. The seat costs more than the site. Site plans are per site, like Webflow's. An agency's tenth client site is a tenth subscription, and add-ons meter on top: $20/mo per 10,000 extra CMS items, $20/mo per 100 extra pages, $40/mo per 100 GB of bandwidth, $20 per locale, and Convert A/B at $50/mo per 500,000 events — where a page view is an event, so the meter runs on ordinary traffic. There is no export. Framer states it outright: "Framer does not offer HTML export for self-hosting." The sharpest form is Workshop, where Framer's AI writes React components for you. You cannot keep the code it wrote you. Verdict: the right pick for a designer producing visually ambitious marketing sites who does not need to own the output. See Blink vs Framer . 3. Squarespace — the best catalogue, and you are renting the design Squarespace's homepage on 18 August 2026 — the "Start for free" line is a trial, not a free plan, and this design is exactly what the XML export leaves behind Blink Price: Basic $19/mo billed annually ($228/yr) · Core $29/mo ($348/yr) · Plus $49/mo ($588/yr) · Advanced $99/mo ($1,188/yr). No free plan — a 14-day trial only. Best for: a brochure site that should look excellent immediately and will not be restructured Nobody has a better catalogue of pre-made templates. Roughly 200 designer-made options let someone with no design skill ship something professional on day one, and SiteBuilderReport rates the design 5/5. Its one genuine advantage over Webflow is buried in a feature list: Core includes unlimited contributors , so the seat problem never arises. The design ceiling is the deal. The same opinionated system that makes it look good is the wall you meet, and on version 7.1 you cannot switch templates after launch . You are renting the design. The export is the sharpest lock-in fact in this comparison. It is a partial, one-way XML file that carries no style settings and no custom CSS — so the design work, the entire reason people choose Squarespace, is precisely what does not survive. You cannot even import it into another Squarespace site. Costs also moved against customers. On 17 July 2026 Squarespace raised prices by up to 26% , notified by email with no public memo, as PetaPixel reported — and Acuity, Member Areas and Email Campaigns are separate subscriptions on top. You cannot edit robots.txt or the sitemap. And Tooltester measured the mobile page-speed score at 28.94, last among the twelve builders they tested . Verdict: the right pick if your site is a beautiful brochure that will not change much. If it has to evolve, you meet the frame. See Blink vs Squarespace . 4. Wix — the widest feature surface, and no way out at all Wix's homepage — the hero sells "the leading website builder" and an Ask Aria panel builds a cycling-club site from a sentence, with no source-code export behind it Blink Price: Light $17/mo · Core $29/mo · Business $39/mo · Business Elite $159/mo, all billed annually. Read first-party from wix.com/plans on 18 August 2026. Best for: a small business that wants bookings, payments, ecommerce and AI in one dashboard and will never move Wix has three advantages a Webflow leaver feels immediately. Ease of use is the best-evidenced: Capterra's Ease of Use sub-score is 4.5 out of 5 across 10,702 reviewers — where Webflow's user rating on the same platform is also 4.5, and it is the editorial reviewers, WebsiteBuilderExpert at 2.1/5, who split them. Wix is also reported to charge 0% platform transaction fees on every plan — a third-party figure whose source we could not open on 18 August 2026, so treat it as unconfirmed by Wix. Business Elite carries 10,000,000 CMS items on a dedicated database, and the SEO controls are substantive rather than cosmetic. Then the wall. Wix's own help centre states a Wix site "needs to be hosted and operated on Wix's servers" because the architecture "does not support external hosting." There is no site or source-code export on the classic Editor or on Wix Studio. Content exports — products, contacts, orders, blog posts as XML. The site does not. If you left Webflow because the export did not carry a working site, Wix does not have one at all. Verdict: the strongest choice if you want every business function in one dashboard and are genuinely comfortable never moving. The year-long breakdown is in best Wix alternatives ; the head-to-head is Blink vs Wix . 5. WordPress + Elementor — the ownership answer, and the agency-volume answer WordPress.com's homepage — the managed face of GPLv2 software you can also run yourself, with SFTP, database and PHP access in the dashboard Blink Price: WordPress.com Personal $4/mo · Premium $8/mo · Business $25/mo · Commerce $45/mo, billed annually. Self-hosted WordPress.org is free GPLv2 software plus hosting and a domain, and Elementor core is a free GPL plugin with 10+ million active installations. Best for: an agency running many small client sites, and anyone who wants nobody able to lock them out, ever On one axis this stack is unbeatable: because WordPress is GPLv2 and you can self-host it, no vendor can hold your site hostage. You own the PHP files and the MySQL database outright, and no plan tier withholds an SEO control — robots.txt, redirects, canonicals and sitemaps are all yours. For an agency, the licensing shape is the argument Webflow cannot answer, because Elementor Pro is licensed by site count: 24x7wpsupport's 2026 breakdown puts Essential at $59/yr for 1 site and Expert at $199/yr for 25 . Read that ladder as unsettled, because three published ladders disagree. wpweblife's guide gives $60 Essential and $108 Advanced, and Elementor's own metadata says "starting from $49/year", so every Elementor figure here is unconfirmed by Elementor . Its pages also disagree about its size: the WordPress.org listing says 22M+ websites, the 20 January 2026 press release says over 21 million. Three costs and a trap. Hosting reprices. SiteGround StartUp goes from $2.99 to $17.99/mo at renewal, a six-fold jump , and WP Rocket and Wordfence recur annually on top. AI is a separate purchase. No classic Pro tier includes AI tools; Elementor One, launched 20 January 2026, is the AI subscription at a reported $15/mo for 1 site and $36/mo for unlimited sites on one credit pool . Security is the cost of the openness. Patchstack recorded 11,334 new vulnerabilities across the WordPress ecosystem in 2025, up 42% year over year — 91% of them in plugins. The trap: Elementor page layouts are its own data, not portable theme markup. Deactivate it and the content stays while the layouts stop rendering. Leaving your host is free. Leaving Elementor means rebuilding the pages. Verdict: correct if ownership beats everything and you have — or are — a developer. See Blink vs WordPress . 6. Ghost™ — the publisher's answer, and it cannot be sold Ghost's members dashboard — total, paid and free members are the headline numbers, because Ghost meters your subscriber list rather than your pages Blink Price: Self-hosted is $0 — MIT-licensed open source, you pay only for infrastructure. Ghost(Pro) Starter $18/mo billed yearly ($216/yr) · Publisher $29/mo yearly ($348/yr at 1,000 members) · Business $199/mo yearly ($2,388/yr). Best for: a publication whose revenue is paid subscriptions If what you run is a publication, Ghost beats any general builder here. Ghost Foundation is a non-profit whose own constitution — its claim, not an audited one — forbids its sale: "the company can never be bought or sold." It publishes live financials — as read on 18 August 2026, $11,055,673 ARR and 30,557 active customers. There is also no published limit on posts, pages or content items , a structural difference from Webflow, Wix and Squarespace. What it meters is members: $29/mo at 1,000, $274 at 100,000 — nine-fold, driven purely by list growth. Those points come from an October 2025 guide whose Starter price has since moved, so trust the shape, not the rungs. Three limits. Custom themes require Publisher, staff users cap at 1 / 3 / 15 by tier, and reviewers name limited customization as the top con — a better writing tool than a design tool, with no store and no data layer. Notably absent: any AI. That is a position, not an oversight. Verdict: if the business is a paid publication, take it. If it is client sites, this is the wrong shape of tool. The three bills Webflow sends you Cost to stay — the real annual bill at 1, 5 and 20 sites At twenty sites the spread across the platforms priced here is $1,219 to $7,200 a year, before anyone does any work. Platform 1 site 5 sites 20 sites Blink $150 $720 Not published — the axis is credits, not sites Webflow $528 $1,728 $6,588 Framer $360 $1,800 $7,200 Squarespace $348 $1,740 $6,960 Wix $348 $1,740 $6,960 WordPress + Elementor $110 $454 $1,219 Ghost(Pro) $348 $1,740 $6,960 Our arithmetic over published annual list prices; seats are a separate axis, priced below. Drivers — Webflow: Premium $300/yr × N plus Workspace Core $228, or Growth $588 at 20 sites. Framer: Pro $360/yr × N, editors extra at $240/editor/yr. Squarespace, Wix, Ghost(Pro): $348/yr × N. WordPress: hosting $36 plus domain $15 per site — that $36 is a promotional first-term rate and reprices at renewal, as the section below sets out — plus one Elementor licence, $59 at 1 site and $199 covering 25, on the ladder published by 24x7wpsupport; Elementor's own pricing page does not render, and three third-party ladders disagree, so treat every Elementor figure here as unconfirmed by Elementor. Each row prices the cheapest tier that carries a CMS and a custom domain, which is why four rows are not the entry tier: Webflow Basic has no CMS at all, Framer Basic caps CMS collections at 2 and gates redirects, staging and search, Wix Light carries no eCommerce, Squarespace Basic levies a 2% commerce fee, and Ghost Starter allows official themes only. Blink's pricing page on 18 August 2026 — the annual toggle takes Starter to $13/mo, Pro to $25 and Max to $100, with credit rollovers gated to Max Blink Blink's row is a different shape and it needs stating, not burying. There is no per-site plan, so site count is not the axis. Traffic is: hosting draws on the same credit pool as building, at 10,000 visits = 50 credits per project per 30 days. One site at that band is 50 credits a month, inside Starter's 100 — $150/yr. Five sites is 250 credits, past Starter's 100 and Pro's 200, so the cheapest published route is a 3-seat Team pooling 300 credits: $720/yr . Twenty sites is roughly 1,000 credits, past the entry rung of both ladders — and Blink publishes only the ends of that ladder, nine rungs from $40 to $3,750 per seat per month, so we will not invent the number in between. What never happens is a linear per-site charge, or a bill for letting the client look at their own site. The site count stops mattering. The traffic does not. WordPress plus Elementor is the cheapest at volume of the platforms compared here , and the catch sits in the same row: those are promotional first-term hosting rates, at renewal the 20-site column becomes roughly $2,899 on Bluehost's renewal rate and about $4,816 on SiteGround's, and you are the operations team for twenty installs. One caveat: readers arriving from the r/webflow threads will also meet open-source, self-hostable visual builders — Webstudio, Nordcraft, Ycode, Plasmic — that we have not priced because they sit outside this comparison, and at least one competes directly on this axis. Cost to leave — what the export actually carries "We can always export later" is said by teams that have never tested the export path. Platform What comes out What breaks Blink Code download, GitHub sync, Dockerfile template — Starter+ Secrets (re-create), database data (separate), edge functions (need Deno) Webflow Static HTML, CSS, JS, assets — needs a paid Workspace CMS (lists empty), forms (submit nowhere), search (dead), ecommerce (cart dead), memberships (gated pages go public) Framer Nothing at all Everything, including the React components its own AI wrote Squarespace Partial one-way XML: layout pages, one blog page, text and image blocks Styles , custom CSS , store , portfolio , events , every blog page after the first Wix Content only — products, contacts, orders, blog XML The site. No source-code export; external hosting unsupported WordPress + Elementor Everything. GPLv2 software, your MySQL database and PHP files Elementor layouts — its own data, not portable markup; deactivate and pages stop rendering Ghost(Pro) Everything, MIT-licensed. JSON export of posts and settings Nothing, but a full move is several artefacts by hand Webflow's export is a design artifact, not a running site — BRIX Templates documents what stops working . There is a real counter-argument on file and it deserves a hearing: a Hacker News commenter has argued Webflow has zero lock-in because it emits static sites with standard semantic HTML. True for a purely static marketing site, false for anything CMS-driven — which is why the honest question is not "can I export" but "what fraction of my site is dynamic." Who edits it after handoff, and what that seat costs Webflow's $180/yr Limited Seat lets your client change CMS text and explicitly cannot touch design, so every layout request comes back to you. Blink's $240/yr member seat changes the design too. Sixty dollars a year is the difference between a handover that ends and one that schedules itself. Platform Free seat Cheapest editing seat What that seat can do Blink Unlimited free viewer seats , consuming no credits Member seat, $240/seat/yr (3-seat minimum) Point-and-click editing, plus full agent access Webflow Reviewer seat, $0, up to 100 per workspace Limited Seat, $180/yr Edit CMS content and publish. Cannot touch design Framer Owner and viewer seats free Content Editor $120/yr; full editor $240/yr CMS, localization and on-page editing. Caps at 10 Squarespace Contributors are not metered $0 — Core includes unlimited contributors Full access within the template Wix Collaborator seats are bundled, not sold per head $0 extra — seats come with the plan Light 2 · Core 5 · Business 10 · Elite 100 collaborators, read first-party 18 August 2026 WordPress + Elementor Unlimited users at no charge $0 — roles are WordPress's own Administrator, Editor, Author, Contributor Ghost(Pro) None — staff seats come with the tier Included by tier: 1 / 3 / 15 staff users Full staff access "Not stated" means the vendor does not publish it and we have not guessed. Read the table without flattering ourselves: on the free-seat row Webflow and Blink are close to a tie , and Squarespace and WordPress beat both of us, because contributors cost nothing at all. What each one can actually do Blink Webflow Framer Squarespace Wix WordPress + Elementor Ghost(Pro) CMS / content ceiling No published limit 20,000 items on Premium* 2,500 items on Pro 1,000 pages, 10,000 products 10M items on Business Elite Your database No published limit Database + end-user auth Both included Auth removed Jan 2026 ; DB via Webflow Cloud only Neither Neither; visitor logins only via the paid Member Areas add-on CMS only; auth not stated Via plugins Members only, not app auth Change it by describing it Yes AI Assistant, metered Canvas agents, metered No Harmony; metering reported, not vendor-confirmed Elementor One, metered No AI at all Robots.txt editable Yes Yes Pro only No Yes Yes Not stated Server-side rendering Not stated by the vendor Yes — semantic server-rendered HTML Yes — pre-rendered at publish Not stated Not stated Yes — PHP Not stated *Webflow's 20,000-item cap is the one figure not confirmed in our 18 August 2026 browser pass; it sits behind a "Compare all Site plans" expander. "Not stated" means the vendor does not publish it and we have not guessed. Webflow, Framer, Ghost, Elementor and Blink checked 18 August 2026; Squarespace, Wix and WordPress 14 August. Moving off Webflow without losing the CMS The export will not carry your CMS, so plan around that fact rather than discovering it. Start by taking what does come out. Export your CMS Collections as CSV while you still have the subscription. The CSV is your content; the static export is a reference, not a running site. Then rebuild from a brief, not from an importer. There is no Webflow importer and we will not imply one — Blink's recorded one-click migrations are Bolt, Lovable, Replit, Emergent and Manus. You describe the site you have and the site you wanted, page by page, and paste the CSV in. Re-create the dynamic layer once, properly. Forms, search, gated content and any member area — the part the export never gave you anyway. Blink ships a per-project SQL database and six sign-in providers in the plan, so gated content does not need the Memberstack-class subscription that Webflow's User Accounts discontinuation pushed people toward. Then the mechanical steps. Review on the preview URL · point your domain by CNAME to cname.blink.new · keep URL paths matching the old ones wherever they earned traffic · run the SEO & AI Search panel · then cancel Webflow. One timing note: Webflow's Freelancer and Agency Workspaces move to the new pricing at renewal on or after 16 November 2026 , other plans from 29 June 2026. Pick by who you are You are an agency shipping polished client sites. Use Blink . What Webflow bills you at twenty sites is the cost side of projects you have already priced, and Blink deletes most of it: the per-client site plan, the per-editor seat, the membership subscription for gated pages, and the unpaid support hours after launch. You bill the same fee and stop buying the cost side of it. That is the margin. It also moves the calendar. A first draft arrives built rather than started and revisions are sentences rather than afternoons, so delivery is days instead of weeks — and the handover ends, because the client changes their own hours and prices without you. One agency owner in the r/webflow price thread put the alternative bluntly: " Webflow is just technical debt at this point. If you sell someone a webflow site you are giving them technical debt that is unnecessary " — r/webflow . If your portfolio is twenty near-identical brochure sites and someone enjoys running servers, self-hosted WordPress with one Elementor Expert licence is cheaper. You are a designer facing the learning curve. Use Blink . The first draft arrives built around what you described, and you refine it by clicking the element or pulling the repo into Cursor. You inherited a Webflow site and cannot edit it. Use Blink . You click the thing on the page and change it, and everyone who only needs to see the site costs nothing. And where we would send you elsewhere. A designer on staff whose job is the website — Webflow. Figma ergonomics with best-in-category motion — Framer. One flawless brochure — Squarespace. Total ownership with a developer to run it — self-hosted WordPress. A paid publication — Ghost. A real store with inventory — Shopify, compared in best Shopify alternatives . Those are good answers to different questions. If your question was how to stop paying per site and per seat for a platform whose exit does not carry a working site, the answer is Blink. Frequently asked questions $528/yr before seats — a Premium Site plan at $300/yr plus a Workspace Core plan at $228/yr, the cheapest tier that includes code export. Seats are separate: $180/yr for a content editor, $468/yr for a designer. Read in a browser, 18 August 2026. Blink, and the reason is the shape of the bill rather than the sticker price. Twenty client sites cost $6,588/yr on Webflow — a $300/yr Premium Site plan per site plus a $588 Growth Workspace — and every person who edits one is a seat on top. Blink has no per-site plan at all: five sites' traffic runs $720/yr on the 3-seat Team plan, adding sites adds credits rather than site plans, and viewer seats are unlimited and free. We do not publish a twenty-site figure because Blink's published ladder skips the rungs in between. The honest exception: if the twenty sites are near-identical brochures and someone enjoys running servers, self-hosted WordPress with one $199 Elementor Expert licence is cheaper at roughly $1,219 a year — before hosting reprices at renewal, and with the caveat that Elementor's own pricing page does not render, so that $199 is third-party-sourced and unconfirmed by Elementor. Self-hosted WordPress with Elementor — roughly $110 for a first year, if you supply the labour. Two things decide whether that is real: promotional hosting reprices up to six-fold at renewal, and you inherit the plugin layer, where Patchstack recorded 11,334 new vulnerabilities in 2025. Blink's Starter at $150/yr includes hosting, a custom domain and a database. Only the open-source ones are free in a way that survives a real site. Elementor core , Ghost and WordPress.org cost nothing to licence — you pay for hosting and a domain. Everything else gates the part you need: Framer's free plan cannot connect a custom domain, Squarespace and Ghost(Pro) have no free plan, Webflow's is a subdomain with ~2 pages, and Blink's is a preview URL. For one buyer, yes, and we are not going to fudge it. If you are a designer who lives on a canvas and produces marketing sites, Framer is the better tool, and its server-rendered output is a genuine architectural advantage nobody should attack. But check the axis you are leaving on: Framer's site plans are per site , exactly like Webflow's, and it adds a seat axis Webflow does not — with no export. Yes, in two shapes. WordPress is GPLv2 and Ghost is MIT-licensed, developed in the open at github.com/TryGhost/Ghost, which showed 54.8k stars on 18 August 2026 — so vendor hostage-taking is impossible for a self-hosted install by construction. On the visual-builder side, readers coming from the r/webflow threads will meet Webstudio, Nordcraft, Ycode and Plasmic; we carry no verified pricing for them and will not invent it. Blink is not open source, but grants full ownership of what you build. Rebuild it, because no automatic converter exists — and take your content out before you cancel. Export each CMS Collection as CSV while the subscription is live; that CSV is the part worth carrying, and the static code export is a reference, not a running site. Then rebuild from a brief: describe the site you have and the site you wanted, page by page, and paste the CSV in. Re-create the dynamic layer once, properly — forms, search, gated content and any member area, all of which the export never carried anyway. Finally review on the preview URL, point the domain by CNAME, keep the URL paths that earned traffic, then cancel Webflow. Partly, and much less than most buyers assume. Export requires a paid Workspace plan. What stops working: Collection lists render empty, forms submit nowhere, search breaks, cart and checkout do not function, and membership login forms die such that previously gated pages become publicly accessible . For a static marketing site the export is usable. For anything CMS-driven it is a design artifact, not a running site. Ghost is a trademark of Ghost Foundation .

title: FedEx Helps Drive a 14% Increase in Colombian Fashion Exports to International Markets
summary: Further strengthening its role as a strategic logistics provider to Colombia's fashion industry, FedEx exported 5.3 million pounds during the last fiscal year, representing a 14% increase in export volume compared to the previous fiscal year.
body_text: Federal Express Corporation, the world’s largest express transportation company, further strengthens its role as a strategic transport service in the international expansion of Colombia’s fashion industry, having exported 5.3 million pounds of apparel, footwear, and fashion products between June 2025 and May 2026. These categories are the company’s second largest vertical industry in the country after flowers. The growth reflects the trust Colombia’s fashion industry places in FedEx logistics capabilities to connect with customers around the world. This milestone comes at a strategic time for the industry. In 2025, Colombia’s fashion and apparel industry recorded US$ 920.6 million in exports. The United States remained the sector’s leading export market, with US$ 255.8 million in exports, representing 27.8% of total export value.[1] This underscores the growth potential of Colombian brands and the importance of working with a trusted carrier like FedEx to help them expand their reach and grow their presence in the U.S. market. To build on this momentum, FedEx in collaboration with Inexmoda, continues to strengthen and expand opportunities through SONNAR, a program designed to support the international growth of Colombian and Latin American brands in the fashion industry. During Colombiamoda Medellín 2026, the country’s premier fashion industry event, the program is supporting Peruvian brand Divina Esencia alongside Colombian brands Agua de Sol , Bibiana Hernández , Barcés , and Misha Shoes , showcasing regional talent and fostering cross-border collaboration to help more companies strengthen their value propositions and expand into new international markets. “Colombiamoda is a key platform for brands across Colombia’s fashion industry to turn their talent and commercial potential into new growth opportunities,” said Ana Lucía López, sales manager for FedEx in Colombia. “At FedEx, we understand that expanding into new markets requires both a strong value proposition and a logistics provider that can support businesses through opportunities, educational resources, visibility, and meaningful business connections. Through SONNAR and our collaboration with Inexmoda, we help brands navigate that journey by providing practical solutions that strengthen their competitiveness.” The 2026 edition of SONNAR received 362 applications, and since the program launched in 2020, nearly 1,000 brands have participated in its initiatives focused on education, visibility, and business networking. To support brands throughout their growth journey, FedEx offers a robust infrastructure and a comprehensive portfolio of logistics solutions. The company operates multiple weekly services from Colombia, including six weekly flights and a dedicated route connecting Bogotá and Medellín with Miami. These services provide businesses with access to the FedEx global network, connecting more than 220 countries and territories. This network is complemented by solutions designed to strengthen the competitiveness of Colombia’s fashion industry and support its continued expansion into international markets. [1] https://analdex.org/2026/06/25/comercio-exterior-sistema-moda-colombia/

title: CareCloud Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results
summary: Revenue Grows 16%; Ninth Consecutive Quarter of Positive GAAP Net Income SOMERSET, N.J., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CareCloud, Inc. (Nasdaq:...
body_text: Revenue Grows 16%; Ninth Consecutive Quarter of Positive GAAP Net Income SOMERSET, N.J., Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CareCloud, Inc. (Nasdaq: CCLD), a leader in AI-powered healthcare technology and revenue cycle management solutions for medical practices and health systems nationwide, today announced financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 and reaffirmed its full-year guidance. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights: Revenue of $31.9 million, compared to $27.4 million in Q2 2025 GAAP net income of $1.1 million, compared to $2.9 million in Q2 2025 GAAP EPS of $0.00 per share, compared to $0.04 per share in Q2 2025 Adjusted EBITDA of $5.9 million, compared to $6.5 million in Q2 2025 Year-to-date 2026 Highlights: Revenue of $63.2 million, compared to $55.0 million in the same period last year GAAP net income of $2.0 million, compared to $4.9 million in the same period last year GAAP EPS of ($0.01) per share, compared to $0.02 per share in the same period last year Adjusted EBITDA of $11.3 million, compared to $12.1 million in the same period last year Key Second Quarter Accomplishments: Compliance and Audit-Defense Market Entry: Expanded the product portfolio through the acquisition of Empower Healthcare & Compliance Partners, opening a new growth opportunity by bringing trusted compliance, audit-defense, and regulatory expertise to CareCloud's network of more than 40,000 providers. Full Redemption of Series B Preferred Stock: Completed the redemption of all outstanding Series B Preferred Stock on May 15, 2026. Sustained Profitability: Delivered the ninth consecutive quarter of positive GAAP net income. Management Commentary “This quarter we grew revenue 16%, delivered our ninth consecutive quarter of positive GAAP net income, and entered the compliance and audit-defense market through our acquisition of Empower Healthcare. We're investing deliberately in what we believe defines our next phase of growth — our AI solutions, our expanding capabilities, and the cross-sell opportunity across our more than 40,000 providers.” — Stephen Snyder, Chief Executive Officer, CareCloud “Our AI and acquisition strategies have become a single, unified growth engine. Every platform we bring into CareCloud becomes smarter, faster, and more valuable when we layer in our AI capabilities. We are still in the early innings of unlocking the cross-sell potential across our expanded client base, and we are increasingly seeing customers adopt our AI-enabled offerings.” — A. Hadi Chaudhry, Chief Strategy Officer, CareCloud "As expected, profitability this quarter reflects deliberate investments we are making today — increased R&D spending on our AI-enabled capabilities and increased interest expense from simplifying our capital structure through the Series B redemption — that we believe will deliver returns over time. We expect these investments to enhance scalability, improve operational efficiency, and support long-term margin expansion." — Norman Roth, Interim Chief Financial Officer and Corporate Controller, CareCloud 2026 Outlook The Company is reaffirming its guidance for calendar year 2026. For the Fiscal Year Ending December 31, 2026 Full Year 2026 Guidance Revenue $128 – $132 million Adjusted EBITDA $29 – $31 million GAAP Net Income Per Share (EPS) $0.20 – $0.23 Our expectations regarding future profitability, including adjusted EBITDA and earnings-per-share guidance, are based on management’s current beliefs and assumptions regarding, among other things, the signing and continuation of certain client and vendor relationships, the anticipated timing and scope of client projects, and our timely execution of integration and expense-management initiatives intended to align our cost structure with those objectives. Explanation of Non-GAAP Financial Measures We report our financial results in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, or GAAP. However, management believes that, in order to properly understand our short-term and long-term financial and operational trends, investors may wish to consider the impact of certain non-cash or non-recurring items, when used as a supplement to financial performance measures in accordance with GAAP. These items result from facts and circumstances that vary in frequency and impact on continuing operations. Management also uses results of operations before such items to evaluate the operating performance of CareCloud and compare it against past periods, make operating decisions and serve as a basis for strategic planning. These non-GAAP financial measures provide management with additional means to understand and evaluate the operating results and trends in our ongoing business by eliminating certain non-cash expenses and other items that management believes might otherwise make comparisons of our ongoing business with prior periods more difficult, obscure trends in ongoing operations, or reduce management’s ability to make useful forecasts. Management believes that these non-GAAP financial measures provide additional means of evaluating period-over-period operating performance. In addition, management understands that some investors and financial analysts find this information helpful in analyzing our financial and operational performance and comparing this performance to our peers and competitors. Management uses adjusted EBITDA, adjusted operating income, adjusted operating margin, and non-GAAP adjusted net income to provide an understanding of aspects of operating results before the impact of investing and financing charges and income taxes. Adjusted EBITDA may be useful to an investor in evaluating our operating performance and liquidity because this measure excludes non-cash expenses as well as expenses pertaining to investing or financing transactions. Management defines “adjusted EBITDA” as the sum of GAAP net income before provision for income taxes, net interest expense, other (income) expense, stock-based compensation expense, depreciation and amortization, integration costs, transaction costs, and change in contingent consideration. Management defines “non-GAAP adjusted operating income” as the sum of GAAP operating income before stock-based compensation expense, amortization of purchased intangible assets, integration costs, transaction costs, and change in contingent consideration, and “non-GAAP adjusted operating margin” as non-GAAP adjusted operating income divided by net revenue. Management defines “non-GAAP adjusted net income” as the sum of GAAP net income before stock-based compensation expense, amortization of purchased intangible assets, other (income) expense, integration costs, transaction costs, change in contingent consideration, any tax impact related to these preceding items and income tax expense related to goodwill, and “non-GAAP adjusted net income per share” as non-GAAP adjusted net income divided by common shares outstanding at the end of the period, including the shares which were issued but are subject to forfeiture and considered contingent consideration. Management considers all of these non-GAAP financial measures to be important indicators of our operational strength and performance of our business and a good measure of our historical operating trends, in particular the extent to which ongoing operations impact our overall financial performance. In addition to items routinely excluded from non-GAAP EBITDA, management excludes or adjusts each of the items identified below from the applicable non-GAAP financial measure referenced above for the reasons set forth with respect to that excluded item: Foreign exchange loss/other expense . Other expense is excluded because foreign currency gains and losses and other non-operating expenses are expenditures that management does not consider part of ongoing operating results when assessing the performance of our business, and also because the total amount of the expense is partially outside of our control. Foreign currency gains and losses are based on global market factors which are unrelated to our performance during the period in which the gains and losses are recorded. Stock-based compensation expense . Stock-based compensation expense is excluded because this is primarily a non-cash expenditure that management does not consider part of ongoing operating results when assessing the performance of our business, and also because the total amount of the expenditure is partially outside of our control because it is based on factors such as stock price, volatility, and interest rates, which may be unrelated to our performance during the period in which the expenses are incurred. Amortization of purchased intangible assets . Purchased intangible assets are amortized over their estimated useful lives and generally cannot be changed or influenced by management after the acquisition. Accordingly, this item is not considered by management in making operating decisions. Management does not believe such charges accurately reflect the performance of our ongoing operations for the period in which such charges are recorded. Contingent consideration. Contingent consideration represents the portion of consideration payable to the seller of some of our acquisitions, the amount of which is based on the achievement of defined performance measures contained in the purchase agreements. Contingent consideration is adjusted to fair value at the end of each reporting period. Management does not believe such charges accurately reflect the performance of our ongoing operations for the period in which such charges are incurred. Transaction costs . Transaction costs are upfront costs related to acquisitions and related transactions, such as brokerage fees, pre-acquisition accounting costs and legal fees, and other upfront costs related to specific transactions. Management believes that such expenses do not have a direct correlation to future business operations, and therefore, these costs are not considered by management in making operating decisions. Management does not believe such charges accurately reflect the performance of our ongoing operations for the period in which such charges are incurred. Integration costs . Integration costs are severance payments for certain employees relating to our acquisitions and exit costs related to terminating leases and other contractual agreements. Accordingly, management believes that such expenses do not have a direct correlation to future business operations, and therefore, these costs are not considered by management in making operating decisions. Management does not believe such charges accurately reflect the performance of our ongoing operations for the period in which such charges are incurred. Restructuring costs . Restructuring costs primarily consist of severance and separation costs associated with the optimization of the Company’s operations and profitability improvements. Management believes that such expenses do not have a direct correlation to future business operations, and therefore, these costs are not considered by management in making operating decisions. Management does not believe such charges accurately reflect the performance of our ongoing operations for the period in which such charges are incurred. Income tax expense related to goodwill. Income tax expense resulting from the amortization of goodwill related to our acquisitions represents a charge to record the tax effect resulting from amortizing goodwill over 15 years for tax purposes. Goodwill is not amortized for GAAP reporting. This expense is not anticipated to result in a cash payment. Free cash flow. Management believes that free cash flow, which measures our ability to generate additional cash from our business operations, is an important financial measure for use in evaluating the Company's financial performance. Free cash flow should be considered in addition to, rather than as a substitute for, consolidated net operating results as a measure of our performance and net cash provided by operating activities as a measure of our liquidity. Additionally, the Company's definition of free cash flow is limited, in that it does not represent residual cash flows available for discretionary expenditures, due to the fact that the measure does not deduct the payments required for debt service and other contractual obligations or payments made for business acquisitions. Therefore, we believe it is important to view free cash flow as a measure that provides supplemental information to our condensed consolidated statements of cash flows.

body_text: More than 75 percent of organizations face costly setbacks due to weak information security controls. Defining ISO 27001 Consulting and Its Purpose ISO 27001 consulting is a specialized strategic service designed to help organizations establish, implement, maintain, and continuously improve their Information Security Management System (ISMS). According to nqcab , this approach is fundamentally a risk management tool that enables businesses to systematically identify, evaluate, and mitigate information security risks across their entire operational landscape. At its core, ISO 27001 consulting focuses on three critical objectives: Identifying strategic, obvious, and hidden information security risks Designing organizational processes to inherently manage those risks Creating adaptive mechanisms to respond and reduce risk exposure The primary purpose of ISO 27001 consulting extends beyond mere compliance. cloudsecurityalliance emphasizes that it involves conducting mandatory independent evaluations to improve an organization's Information Security Management System's effectiveness. Consultants work closely with organizations to ensure their ISMS meets rigorous international standards while developing robust strategies that protect critical business information assets. Successful ISO 27001 consulting transforms information security from a reactive, checkbox exercise into a proactive, strategic business function. By providing expert guidance, consultants help organizations build resilient security frameworks that not only protect against current threats but also anticipate and adapt to emerging cybersecurity challenges. Types of ISO 27001 Consulting Services Available ISO 27001 consulting encompasses a wide range of specialized services designed to help organizations develop comprehensive Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). starconsulting highlights that experienced consultants provide critical support that goes beyond standard implementation, offering transformative benefits for businesses seeking robust cybersecurity frameworks. The most common types of ISO 27001 consulting services include: Gap Analysis Consulting : Identifying current security weaknesses and compliance gaps ISMS Design and Implementation : Developing customized security management systems Risk Assessment Services : Conducting thorough risk evaluations and mitigation strategies Documentation and Policy Development : Creating comprehensive security documentation Training and Awareness Programs : Educating organizational staff on security best practices Internal Audit Preparation : Preparing organizations for formal ISO 27001 certification audits According to grcguru , specialized consulting services extend across multiple industry sectors, including: Automotive Cybersecurity (ISO/SAE 21434, TiSAX) Industrial Control Systems and Operational Technology (ISA/IEC 62443) Healthcare Systems Security (FDA QSR, GxP compliance) The ultimate goal of these diverse consulting services is to transform information security from a compliance requirement into a strategic business advantage. By providing tailored guidance, ISO 27001 consultants help organizations build resilient, adaptive security frameworks that protect critical assets while enabling business growth and innovation. Core Phases of the ISO 27001 Consulting Process The ISO 27001 consulting process is a structured, methodical approach to developing and implementing a robust Information Security Management System (ISMS). starconsulting outlines five critical phases that organizations must navigate to achieve comprehensive information security maturity. These core phases include: Development of Project Plan : Establishing clear objectives, scope, and strategic alignment Review and Gap Assessment : Identifying current security vulnerabilities and compliance shortfalls Process Mapping and Management System Development : Designing tailored security frameworks Management System Implementation : Executing and integrating security controls Internal Assessment and Management Review : Continuously evaluating and improving the ISMS nqcab emphasizes that a detailed action plan supported by regular reviews and monitoring provides the most compelling evidence of a well-structured system during audits. Risk assessment remains the cornerstone of an effective ISMS, enabling organizations to proactively identify, evaluate, and mitigate potential security threats. Successful implementation of these phases transforms information security from a reactive compliance exercise into a strategic, adaptive framework. By methodically addressing each phase, organizations can build resilient security systems that not only protect critical assets but also demonstrate a commitment to continuous improvement and organizational excellence. Key Roles, Responsibilities, and Obligations ISO 27001 consulting requires a comprehensive approach to defining and allocating critical roles within an organization's Information Security Management System (ISMS). cloudsecurityalliance emphasizes that the internal audit function plays a mandatory, independent role in evaluating and improving the effectiveness of the ISMS. Key roles and responsibilities typically include: Top Management : Strategic oversight and commitment to information security Information Security Manager : Direct responsibility for ISMS implementation and maintenance Risk Management Team : Identifying, assessing, and mitigating information security risks Internal Auditors : Conducting independent evaluations of ISMS effectiveness Data Owners : Responsible for specific data assets and their protection Compliance Officers : Ensuring adherence to ISO 27001 standards and regulatory requirements nqcab highlights that the fundamental obligation of these roles is to manage organizational risks comprehensively. This involves identifying strategic, obvious, and hidden information security risks while ensuring that day-to-day activities and processes are designed to inherently manage those risks. Successful implementation requires a collaborative approach where each role understands its specific obligations. Organizations must create a culture of shared responsibility, where information security is not just a technical requirement but a strategic imperative. This means continuous adaptation, proactive risk management, and a commitment to reducing the organization's overall risk exposure through coordinated efforts across all levels of the organization. Common Challenges and Mistakes in ISO 27001 Consulting nqcab emphasizes that ISO 27001 consulting is fundamentally a risk management process that requires organizations to systematically identify and address information security challenges. However, many businesses encounter critical mistakes that can undermine their Information Security Management System (ISMS) implementation. Common challenges and mistakes include: Superficial Risk Assessment : Failing to comprehensively identify strategic, obvious, and hidden security risks Inadequate Management Commitment : Treating ISO 27001 as a compliance checkbox rather than a strategic initiative Incomplete Documentation : Creating generic, non-specific security policies that lack practical application Overlooking Continuous Improvement : Viewing the ISMS as a static framework instead of an adaptive system Insufficient Training : Not investing in comprehensive staff awareness and skill development Neglecting Regular Internal Audits : Failing to consistently evaluate and refine security processes cloudsecurityalliance highlights that the internal audit is a mandatory, independent activity crucial for evaluating and improving ISMS effectiveness. Organizations often make the mistake of treating this as a perfunctory exercise rather than a strategic opportunity for continuous risk management and security enhancement. Successful ISO 27001 consulting requires a holistic, dynamic approach that goes beyond mere compliance. Organizations must develop an adaptive security framework that can automatically respond to emerging threats, continuously reduce risk exposure, and integrate security deeply into their day-to-day operational processes. By recognizing and addressing these common challenges, businesses can transform their approach from reactive protection to proactive risk management. Benefits and ROI of Professional ISO 27001 Consulting starconsulting reveals that professional ISO 27001 consulting delivers substantial strategic advantages beyond traditional compliance measures. An experienced consultant transforms an organization's approach to information security, creating a robust framework that directly impacts operational efficiency and business opportunities. Key benefits of professional ISO 27001 consulting include: Enhanced Risk Management : Systematic identification and mitigation of security vulnerabilities Increased Business Credibility : Demonstrating commitment to robust information security practices Competitive Differentiation : Standing out in markets that prioritize data protection Operational Efficiency : Streamlining security processes and reducing potential disruptions Cost Reduction : Preventing potential security breaches and associated financial losses Strategic Alignment : Developing security frameworks tailored to specific organizational needs grcguru highlights the comprehensive nature of these consulting services, which extend across multiple industry sectors including automotive, industrial control systems, and healthcare. The return on investment (ROI) becomes evident through reduced implementation time, improved risk profiles, and increased organizational resilience. Ultimately, professional ISO 27001 consulting is not an expense but a strategic investment. title: The kefir renaissance
summary: Kefir has moved from regional specialty to one of dairy’s fastest-growing categories. Global launches rose 15.7% in the first half of 2025 (Mintel GNPD), driven by gut health, demand for traditional fermentation and a wave... The post The kefir renaissance appeared first on IFF .
body_text: Kefir has moved from regional specialty to one of dairy’s fastest-growing categories. Global launches rose 15.7% in the first half of 2025 (Mintel GNPD), driven by gut health, demand for traditional fermentation and a wave of new formats. For manufacturers, the opportunity now sits in how consistently that experience can be delivered. Why one of the world’s oldest fermented drinks is becoming one of dairy’s biggest opportunities Few fermented dairy products have traveled a journey quite like kefir . Originating in the Caucasus Mountains, where kefir grains were traditionally used to ferment milk into what became known as the ‘drink of bliss’, kefir remained a regional specialty for centuries. Today, however, it is emerging as one of the most dynamic categories in cultured dairy, driven by consumers looking for foods that combine fermentation heritage, functional nutrition and authentic provenance. For dairy manufacturers, the resurgence of kefir represents far more than another product trend. It reflects a convergence of long-term consumer shifts that continue to reshape the cultured dairy category and create new opportunities for innovation. That momentum is increasingly visible on supermarket shelves around the world. According to Mintel GNPD , global kefir launches increased by 15.7% during the first half of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024, while established brands and retailers continue to expand their portfolios across Europe, North America and Asia. In the UK, a range of companies have introduced new kefir products in response to growing consumer demand for fermented dairy and digestive wellness. A category driven by multiple consumer trends Interest in gut health remains one of the strongest drivers of functional food innovation, with consumers increasingly recognizing the relationship between digestive health and overall wellbeing. At the same time, demand continues to grow for products perceived as minimally processed, familiar and made using traditional production methods. Kefir occupies a unique position at the intersection of these trends, offering a product with centuries of heritage alongside a fermentation process that consumers increasingly associate with authenticity and wellness. Manufacturers are also benefiting from consumers seeking products that deliver multiple benefits within a single purchase decision. Alongside digestive wellness, brands are increasingly positioning kefir around protein, fiber and broader functional nutrition, with recent launches including high-protein formulations, kefir shots, products containing added inulin, and even beverages supporting cognitive health. Rather than being confined to the dairy aisle, kefir is becoming part of a broader movement toward everyday functional nutrition. Innovation is expanding the boundaries of kefir Innovation is also reshaping the category itself. Traditional plain kefir continues to perform strongly, particularly across Eastern Europe, but manufacturers are rapidly expanding into fruit variants, indulgent dessert-inspired flavors, sparkling beverages and frozen desserts. Plant-based kefir, produced from alternative substrates including coconut and grains, is opening the category to entirely new consumer groups. The result is that kefir is no longer a single product with a single consumer. It has become a versatile fermentation platform capable of addressing a wide range of health, lifestyle and sensory preferences. Kefir growth creates new manufacturing challenges As consumer expectations continue to evolve, so too do the demands placed on manufacturers. Although consumers increasingly value kefir for its fermentation heritage, very few appreciate the complexity required to produce it consistently at commercial scale. Traditional kefir is created through the symbiotic fermentation of milk by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts contained within kefir grains, creating a living microbial ecosystem that develops the product’s characteristic flavor, texture and gentle carbonation. Unlike many cultured dairy products, those microorganisms continue to interact throughout production and storage, making kefir one of the most technically demanding fermented dairy products to manufacture consistently. For manufacturers, every decision influences the final product: Fermentation temperature affects flavor intensity and gas formation, Maturation helps develop the characteristic sensory profile Cooling conditions, milk composition and processing methods all contribute to texture, acidity and shelf-life performance. Even seemingly small adjustments can produce noticeable differences in flavor, mouthfeel and consumer perception. These challenges become even more significant as manufacturers seek to innovate. Developing a high-protein kefir, reducing carbonation for consumers unfamiliar with traditional products, or creating formulations for different regional markets all require careful control of the fermentation process without losing the authenticity that makes kefir unique. From opportunity to competitive advantage Successfully responding to these challenges requires much more than following market trends. It demands a deep understanding of fermentation science and the ability to translate that knowledge into products that consistently meet consumer expectations. This is where experience becomes a genuine competitive advantage. With more than 80 years of expertise in fermentation and one of the industry’s broadest portfolios of kefir cultures, IFF works with dairy manufacturers around the world to help translate consumer insights into commercially successful products. Our portfolio spans traditional cultures produced from f reeze-dried kefir grains through to multi-species culture systems designed to deliver specific flavor, texture, shelf-life and processing characteristics, allowing manufacturers to create products tailored to local markets while maintaining consistent production performance. As consumer interest in kefir continues to accelerate, the question is no longer whether there is an opportunity within the category, but how manufacturers can differentiate themselves while delivering the authentic sensory experience consumers increasingly expect. Ready to unlock the next generation of Kefir Innovation? Contact our experts to get started. More about our Fresh Dairy Cultures & Enzymes. The post The kefir renaissance appeared first on IFF .
