body_text: View All News Mattel Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results August 4, 2026 Second Quarter 2026 Highlights Versus Prior Year Net Sales of $1,125 million, up 10% as reported, and 9% in constant currency Gross Margin of 48.2%, a decrease of 270 basis points; Adjusted Gross Margin of 48.6%, a decrease of 260 basis points Operating Income of $11 million, a decrease of $68 million; Adjusted Operating Income of $39 million, a decrease of $57 million Net Loss of $18 million, compared to Net Income of $53 million Loss per Share of $0.06 compared to Earnings per Share of $0.16; Adjusted Earnings per Share of $0.01 compared to $0.21 per share Business Highlights Positive consumer demand for our products year-to-date Released Masters of the Universe movie globally Launched first self-published mobile game establishing publishing and digital customer acquisition capabilities; second game in soft launch Integration of Mattel163 mobile games studio progressing well Company reiterates 2026 guidance; reaffirms 2026 share repurchase target of $400 million EL SEGUNDO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Mattel, Inc. (NASDAQ: MAT) today reported second quarter 2026 financial results. Ynon Kreiz, Chairman and CEO of Mattel, said: “We continued to execute our multi-year strategy to grow our IP-driven play and family entertainment business in the second quarter with strong growth in Net Sales. Growth has continued in the third quarter, and we expect to achieve our full year 2026 guidance. Our world-class brand portfolio and product offering, driven by our brand-centric operating model and global capabilities, position us well for the second half of the year.” Paul Ruh, CFO of Mattel, added: “Mattel achieved further savings from our three-year Optimizing for Profitable Growth program, which is on track to achieve $225 million of savings by year-end. In line with our capital allocation priorities, we are making strategic investments to accelerate growth and repurchased another $100 million of shares in the quarter, bringing the year-to-date total to $300 million of shares, and we continue to expect repurchases of $400 million in total this year, while maintaining a strong balance sheet.” Second Quarter Financial Overview Net Sales Net Sales were $1,125 million, up 10% as reported, and 9% in constant currency, versus the prior year’s second quarter. The increase in Net Sales as reported was driven by a 12% increase in North America and a 9% increase in International. The increase in Net Sales in constant currency was driven by a 12% increase in North America and a 5% increase in International. Gross Margin Reported Gross Margin was 48.2%, versus 50.9% in the prior year’s second quarter, and Adjusted Gross Margin was 48.6%, versus 51.2%. The decrease in Reported and Adjusted Gross Margin was primarily due to the gross incremental cost of tariffs, inflation, higher royalties, and unfavorable foreign exchange, partially offset by the contribution of Mattel163, and Other, including tariff mitigation actions and cost savings. Operating Income Reported Operating Income was $11 million, a decrease of $68 million, and Adjusted Operating Income was $39 million, a decrease of $57 million. The decrease in Reported and Adjusted Operating Income was primarily due to higher Advertising and SG&A expenses, as well as lower gross margin, partly offset by higher Net Sales. Earnings Per Share Reported Earnings per Share was a loss of $0.06, as compared to income of $0.16, and Adjusted Earnings per Share was $0.01, as compared to $0.21. The decrease in Reported and Adjusted Earnings per Share was primarily due to the same factors that impacted Operating Income. As of June 30, 2026, shares outstanding totaled 285.7 million. Cash Flow For the six months ended June 30, 2026, Cash Flows Used for Operating Activities were $202 million, as compared to a use of $275 million, primarily due to favorable working capital usage, partially offset by a decrease in Net Income, excluding the impact of non-cash items. Cash Flows Used for Investing Activities were $195 million, compared to a use of $55 million, primarily due to cash paid in connection with the acquisition of Mattel163 net of cash acquired, and higher capital expenditures. Cash Flows Used for Financing Activities and Other were $322 million, as compared to a use of $188 million, primarily due to an increase in share repurchases and the impact of foreign currency exchange rate changes on cash. Second Quarter Gross Billings by Category Worldwide Gross Billings for Dolls were $318 million, down 5% as reported, or 7% in constant currency, primarily due to a decline in Barbie. Worldwide Gross Billings for Vehicles were $463 million, up 14% as reported, or 11% in constant currency, primarily driven by growth in Hot Wheels. Worldwide Gross Billings for Infant, Toddler, and Preschool were $128 million, down 11% as reported, or 13% in constant currency, primarily due to a decline in Fisher-Price. Worldwide Gross Billings for Action Figures, Building Sets, Games, and Other were $358 million, up 35% as reported, or 33% in constant currency, primarily driven by growth in Games (including the contribution of Digital Games, following the full acquisition of Mattel163) and Action Figures, driven by theatrical releases. 2026 Guidance Mattel’s full year 2026 guidance remains: (in millions, except EPS and percentages) FY2026 Guidance FY2025 Actual Net Sales +3% to 6%* $5,348 Adjusted Gross Margin Approx. 50% 48.9% Adjusted Operating Income $580 - $630 $652 Adjusted Tax Rate Approx. 24% 20% Adjusted EPS $1.27 - $1.39 $1.49 * in Constant Currency Our guidance remains subject to market volatility, unexpected disruptions, as well as other macro-economic risks and uncertainties, including further developments in the Middle East and regulatory actions impacting global trade. Guidance does not include any potential impact of tariff refunds. A reconciliation of Mattel’s non-GAAP financial measures on a forward-looking basis, including Net Sales on a constant currency basis, Adjusted Gross Margin, Adjusted Operating Income, Adjusted Tax Rate, Adjusted EPS, and Free Cash Flow, is not available without unreasonable effort. Mattel is unable to predict with sufficient certainty items that would be excluded from the corresponding GAAP measures, including the effect of foreign currency exchange rate fluctuations, unusual gains and losses or charges, and severance and restructuring charges, due to the unpredictable nature of such items, which may have a significant impact on Mattel’s GAAP measures. Conference Call and Live Webcast At 5:00 p.m. (Eastern Daylight Time) today, Mattel will host a conference call with investors and financial analysts to discuss its latest financial results. The conference call will be webcast on Mattel's Investor Relations website, https://investors.mattel.com . To listen to the live call, log on to the website at least 10 minutes early to register, download, and install any necessary audio software. An archive of the webcast will be available on Mattel's Investor Relations website for 12 months and may be accessed beginning approximately three hours after the completion of the live call. Forward-Looking Statements This press release contains a number of forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Forward-looking statements can be identified by the fact that they do not relate strictly to historical or current facts or by their nature are uncertain, and include statements regarding Mattel’s guidance and goals for future periods and other future events. The use of words such as “anticipates,” “expects,” “intends,” “plans,” “projects,” “looks forward,” “confident that,” “believes,” and “targeted,” among others, generally identify forward-looking statements. These forward-looking statements are based on currently available operating, financial, economic, and other information and assumptions, and are subject to a number of significant risks and uncertainties. A variety of factors or combination of factors, many of which are beyond Mattel’s control, may cause actual results or outcomes, or the timing of those results or outcomes, to differ materially from those contained in any forward-looking statements. Specific factors that might cause such a difference include, but are not limited to: (i) Mattel’s ability to design, develop, produce, manufacture, source, ship, and distribute products in a timely and cost-effective manner; (ii) sufficient interest in and demand for the products and entertainment Mattel offers by retail customers and consumers to profitably recover Mattel’s costs; (iii) downturns in economic conditions affecting Mattel’s markets which can negatively impact retail customers and consumers, and which can result in lower employment levels and lower consumer disposable income and spending, including lower spending on purchases of Mattel’s products; (iv) other factors which can lower discretionary consumer spending, such as higher costs for fuel and food, drops in the value of homes or other consumer assets, and high levels of consumer debt; (v) potential difficulties or delays Mattel may experience in implementing cost savings and efficiency enhancing initiatives; (vi) other economic and public health conditions or regulatory changes in the markets in which Mattel and its customers and suppliers operate, which could create delays or increase Mattel’s costs, such as higher commodity prices, labor costs, transportation costs, or outbreaks of disease; (vii) the effect of inflation on Mattel’s business, including cost inflation in supply chain inputs and increased labor costs, as well as pricing actions taken in an effort to mitigate the effects of inflation; (viii) currency fluctuations, including movements in foreign exchange rates, which can lower Mattel’s net revenues and earnings, and significantly impact Mattel’s costs; (ix) the concentration of Mattel’s customers, potentially increasing the negative impact to Mattel of difficulties experienced by any of Mattel’s customers, such as bankruptcies or liquidations or a general lack of success, or changes in their purchasing or selling patterns; (x) the inventory policies of Mattel’s retail customers, as well as the concentration of Mattel’s revenues in the second half of the year, which, coupled with reliance by retailers on quick response inventory management techniques, increases the risk of underproduction, overproduction, and shipping delays; (xi) legal, reputational, and financial risks related to security breaches or cyberattacks; (xii) work disruptions, including as a result of supply chain disruption such as plant or port closures, which may impact Mattel’s ability to manufacture or deliver product in a timely and cost-effective manner; Presentation Information / Non-GAAP Financial Measures The financial results included herein are preliminary until Mattel’s Form 10-Q is filed with the SEC. Actual results may differ from these preliminary results. To supplement our financial results presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles in the United States (“GAAP”), Mattel presents certain non-GAAP financial measures within the meaning of Regulation G promulgated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The non-GAAP financial measures that Mattel uses in this earnings release include Adjusted Gross Profit, Adjusted Gross Margin, Adjusted Other Selling and Administrative Expenses, Adjusted Operating Income/Loss, Adjusted Operating Income/Loss Margin, Adjusted Earnings Per Share, earnings before interest expense, taxes, depreciation and amortization (“EBITDA”), Adjusted EBITDA, Free Cash Flow, Free Cash Flow Conversion (Free Cash Flow / Adjusted EBITDA), Leverage Ratio (Total Debt / Adjusted EBITDA), Net Debt, Adjusted Tax Rate, and constant currency. Mattel uses these measures to analyze its continuing operations and to monitor, assess, and identify meaningful trends in its operating and financial performance, and each is discussed below. Mattel believes that the disclosure of non-GAAP financial measures provides useful supplemental information to investors to be able to better evaluate ongoing business performance and certain components of Mattel’s results. These measures are not, and should not be viewed as, substitutes for GAAP financial measures and may not be comparable to similarly titled measures used by other companies. Reconciliations of the non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP financial measures are attached to this earnings release as exhibits and to our earnings slide presentation as an appendix. This earnings release and our earnings slide presentation are available on Mattel's Investor Relations website, https://investors.mattel.com/ , under the subheading “Financials – Quarterly Results.” Adjusted Gross Profit and Adjusted Gross Margin Adjusted Gross Profit and Adjusted Gross Margin represent reported Gross Profit and reported Gross Margin, respectively, adjusted to exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets, severance and restructuring expenses, and acquisition-related expenses, including integration expenses. Adjusted Gross Margin represents Mattel’s Adjusted Gross Profit, as a percentage of Net Sales. Adjusted Gross Profit and Adjusted Gross Margin are presented to provide additional perspective on underlying trends in Mattel’s core Gross Profit and Gross Margin, which Mattel believes is useful supplemental information for investors to be able to gauge and compare Mattel’s current business performance from one period to another. Adjusted Other Selling and Administrative Expenses Adjusted Other Selling and Administrative Expenses represents Mattel’s reported Other Selling and Administrative Expenses, adjusted to exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets, severance and restructuring expenses, the impact of the inclined sleeper product recalls, and acquisition-related expenses, including professional fees and integration expenses, which are not part of Mattel’s core business. Adjusted Other Selling and Administrative Expenses is presented to provide additional perspective on underlying trends in Mattel’s core other selling and administrative expenses, which Mattel believes is useful supplemental information for investors to be able to gauge and compare Mattel’s current business performance from one period to another. Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) Margin Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) Margin represent reported Operating Income and reported Operating Income Margin, respectively, adjusted to exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets, severance and restructuring expenses, the impact of the inclined sleeper product recalls, and acquisition-related expenses, including professional fees and integration expenses, which are not part of Mattel’s core business. Adjusted Operating Income Margin represents Mattel’s Adjusted Operating Income, as a percentage of Net Sales. Adjusted Operating Income and Adjusted Operating Income Margin are presented to provide additional perspective on underlying trends in Mattel’s core operating results, which Mattel believes is useful supplemental information for investors to be able to gauge and compare Mattel’s current business performance from one period to another. Adjusted Earnings Per Share Adjusted Earnings Per Share represents Mattel’s reported Diluted Earnings Per Common Share, adjusted to exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets, severance and restructuring expenses, the impact of the inclined sleeper product recalls, acquisition-related expenses, net, including professional fees and integration expenses, and gain on previously held equity interest in Mattel163, which are not part of Mattel’s core business. The aggregate tax effect of the adjustments was determined using the effective tax rates on a jurisdictional basis of the respective adjustments and dividing by the reported weighted-average number of common shares. Adjusted Earnings Per Share is presented to provide additional perspective on underlying trends in Mattel’s core business. Mattel believes it is useful supplemental information for investors to gauge and compare Mattel’s current earnings results from one period to another. Adjusted Earnings Per Share is a performance measure and should not be used as a measure of liquidity. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA EBITDA represents Mattel’s Net Income/Loss, adjusted to exclude the impact of interest expense, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. Adjusted EBITDA represents EBITDA adjusted to exclude share-based compensation, severance and restructuring expenses, the impact of the inclined sleeper product recalls, acquisition-related expenses, net, including professional fees and integration expenses, and gain on previously held equity interest in Mattel163, which are not part of Mattel’s core business. Mattel believes EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are useful supplemental information for investors to gauge and compare Mattel’s business performance to other companies in its industry with similar capital structures. The presentation of Adjusted EBITDA differs from how Mattel calculates EBITDA for purposes of covenant compliance under the indentures governing its high yield senior notes and the revolving credit agreement governing its revolving credit facility. Because of these limitations, EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA should not be considered as measures of discretionary cash available to invest in the growth of Mattel’s business. As a result, Mattel relies primarily on its GAAP results and uses EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA only supplementally. Free Cash Flow and Free Cash Flow Conversion Free Cash Flow represents Mattel’s net cash flows from operating activities less capital expenditures. Free Cash Flow Conversion represents Mattel’s free cash flow divided by Adjusted EBITDA. Mattel believes Free Cash Flow and Free Cash Flow Conversion are useful supplemental information for investors to gauge Mattel’s liquidity and performance and to compare Mattel’s business performance to other companies in our industry. Free Cash Flow does not represent cash available to Mattel for discretionary expenditures. Leverage Ratio (Total Debt / Adjusted EBITDA) The leverage ratio is calculated by dividing Total Debt by Adjusted EBITDA. Total Debt represents the aggregate of Mattel’s current portion of long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and long-term debt, excluding the impact of debt issuance costs and debt discount. Mattel believes the leverage ratio is useful supplemental information for investors to gauge trends in Mattel’s business and to compare Mattel’s business performance to other companies in its industry. Net Debt Net Debt represents the aggregate of Mattel’s current portion of long-term debt, short-term borrowings, and long-term debt, less cash and equivalents. Mattel believes Net Debt is useful supplemental information for investors to monitor Mattel’s liquidity and evaluate its balance sheet. Adjusted Tax Rate The Adjusted Tax Rate is calculated by dividing Adjusted Provision for Income Taxes by Adjusted Income Before Income Taxes. Adjusted Income Before Income Taxes represents reported Income Before Income Taxes, adjusted to exclude amortization of acquired intangible assets, severance and restructuring expenses, the impact of inclined sleeper product recalls, acquisition-related expenses, net, and gain on previously held equity interest in Mattel163. The Adjusted Provision for Income Taxes represents reported Provision for Income Taxes, adjusted to exclude the aggregate tax effect of adjustments. Mattel believes the adjusted tax rate provides useful supplemental information for investors to gauge and compare the impact of tax expense on Mattel's earnings results from one period to another. Constant Currency Percentage changes in results expressed in constant currency are presented excluding the impact from changes in currency exchange rates. To present this information, Mattel calculates constant currency information by translating current period and prior period results for entities reporting in currencies other than the US dollar using consistent exchange rates. The constant currency exchange rates are determined by Mattel at the beginning of each year and are applied consistently during the year. They are generally different from the actual exchange rates in effect during the current or prior period due to volatility in actual foreign exchange rates. Mattel considers whether any changes to the constant currency rates are appropriate at the beginning of each year. The exchange rates used for these constant currency calculations are generally based on prior year actual exchange rates. The difference between the current period and prior period results using the consistent exchange rates reflects the changes in the underlying performance results, excluding the impact from changes in currency exchange rates. Mattel analyzes constant currency results to provide additional perspective on changes in underlying trends in Mattel’s operating performance. Mattel believes that the disclosure of the percentage change in constant currency is useful supplemental information for investors to be able to gauge Mattel’s current business performance and the longer-term strength of its overall business since foreign currency changes could potentially mask underlying sales trends. The disclosure of the percentage change in constant currency enhances investor’s ability to compare financial results from one period to another. Key Performance Indicator Gross Billings Gross Billings represent amounts invoiced to customers. It does not include the impact of sales adjustments, such as trade discounts and other allowances. Mattel presents changes in gross billings as a metric for comparing its aggregate, categorical, brand, and geographic results to highlight significant trends in Mattel’s business. Changes in Gross Billings are discussed because, while Mattel records the details of sales adjustments in its financial accounting systems at the time of sale, such sales adjustments are generally not associated with categories, brands, and individual products. title: Best AI Scribe for Psychiatry: Med Management Guide 2026
summary: Psychiatric notes need structured MSEs, dosing rationale, and correct E/M coding. See what separates a psychiatry-tuned AI scribe from a general medical one.
body_text: A medication management visit is scheduled for 15 minutes. In that window the chart has to end up with the current regimen, dosages, adherence, perceived efficacy, side effects, the rationale for every change, controlled-substance documentation where it applies, refills authorized, the follow-up interval, and patient education [2]. That is ten things from one short visit, and it is why psychiatric notes get finished at 9 p.m. Most ambient AI scribes were built for a primary care encounter. Point one at a med check and you get a readable paragraph that quietly loses the mental status exam and attaches the dose change to the wrong drug. So the question for a prescriber is not whether an AI scribe can transcribe. It is whether it produces a note a prescriber can sign. Key Takeaway: An AI scribe for psychiatry has to do more than transcribe a conversation. A prescriber's note must capture the mental status exam, the current medication regimen with dosages and adherence, side effects and dosing rationale, a structured risk assessment, and controlled-substance documentation where it applies, often from a 15-minute medication management visit. General ambient scribes are tuned for primary care encounters and tend to flatten the MSE and lose dosing detail. The right scribe produces a prescriber-ready note, supports E/M plus psychotherapy add-on coding when both services occur in one visit, and keeps the prescriber as the clinician of record. Sully.ai's AI Scribe writes the note into the EHR and hands it to the AI Coder, which extracts the ICD-10 and CPT codes and submits a clean claim. The Documentation Load Inside a 15-Minute Medication Visit Psychiatry has an unusual ratio. The visit is short, the documentation is not. A follow-up med check produces a longer required record than a comparable 15-minute primary care visit, because the note has to justify prescribing decisions rather than record findings. Every dose change needs a reason. Every controlled substance needs its own trail. Adherence and side effects have to be captured in the patient's own terms, then interpreted. Why the Mental Status Exam Is the Hardest Part to Automate The MSE is not prose. It is a set of defined domains: appearance, behavior, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, cognition, insight, and judgment. A general scribe tends to compress all of that into one or two sentences, because in primary care a brief observation is normal. In psychiatry the MSE is the exam, and a collapsed MSE is a note that does not support the assessment above it. A psychiatry-tuned scribe populates the domains separately [1][3]. Why Polypharmacy Breaks Generic Transcription A prescriber may adjust one agent, hold another, and cross-taper a third inside a single conversation. The sentence "let's go up to 100" only means something when it is attached to the right medication. This is where generic transcription becomes a clinical safety problem rather than a formatting preference. The scribe has to track multiple agents, their dosages, and which one each instruction refers to [3]. What Psychiatric Documentation Requires That General Scribes Miss Four things separate a psychiatric note from a general ambient note. A prescriber evaluating tools should test all four directly. Structured Mental Status Exam and Risk Assessment Beyond the MSE domains, the note needs a risk assessment that separates dynamic factors, static factors, and protective factors, with safety planning documented whenever risk is present. Some psychiatry-focused tools integrate standardized instruments such as the C-SSRS and PHQ-9 or GAD-7 directly into the note [3]. Medication Reconciliation and Dosing Rationale The record has to show what changed, what it changed to, and why. "Increased sertraline to 100mg daily given partial response at 50mg and no adverse effects" is a defensible entry. "Adjusted medications" is not. The E/M Plus Psychotherapy Coding Boundary This is the part almost nobody writes about, and it is where psychiatric notes most often become unbillable. A prescriber's follow-up is not a psychotherapy visit. It bills an evaluation and management code , 99212 to 99215 for an established patient or 99202 to 99205 for a new one, selected on medical decision making or on total time for the date of the encounter [4]. If you also delivered psychotherapy in that same visit, you add a psychotherapy add-on code on top of the E/M: +90833 for 16 to 37 minutes, +90836 for 38 to 52 minutes, or +90838 for 53 minutes or more. The psychotherapy minutes are counted separately from the E/M work , which means the note has to document the two components separately, each with its own time element [4]. Here is the trap. You cannot report a stand-alone psychotherapy code (90832, 90834, 90837) alongside an E/M service on the same date. It denies as a duplicate service [4]. Those stand-alone codes are the therapy-only path, and a prescriber who reaches for them after a med check is filing a claim that will come back. The initial evaluation follows different rules again: 90791 is the diagnostic evaluation without medical services, and 90792 includes medical services and is the usual code for a prescriber. Neither one is time-based, so the note has to carry the clinical elements rather than lean on a time total [4]. None of that is a transcription problem. It is a structuring problem. Most ambient scribes produce one continuous narrative and leave the prescriber to split it apart afterward, which is exactly the manual work the tool was supposed to remove. Telehealth Adds Fields the Note Has to Carry If any of your visits are virtual, the note also needs the place of service code, the right modifier, whether the encounter was audio-video or audio-only, the patient's location, your location, and telehealth consent. Those are easy to omit and easy for a payer to spot. Every template linked below has them as explicit fields. Confidentiality Rules That Go Beyond HIPAA Substance use treatment records are governed by 42 CFR Part 2, which is stricter than HIPAA [3]. If your practice touches addiction medicine at all, ask any vendor about it explicitly rather than accepting a general HIPAA answer. Free Psychiatry Note Templates If you want the structure without the software, these are the four formats a psychiatric practice actually uses. Each one has the payer requirements written into the page: clock times plus total time, the encounter and coding fields including place of service and telehealth modifiers, the diagnosis to impairment to intervention link, means access in the risk section, and an attestation block for signature and credentials. Psychiatry SOAP note template for medication management and follow-up, keeping what the patient reported separate from what you observed Psychiatric intake evaluation template for the initial evaluation, three pages, the note that establishes medical necessity for the entire course of treatment DAP note template for the therapy portion of a combined visit Behavioral health BIRP note template for community mental health and public payer settings, where interventions must tie to treatment plan goals How to Evaluate an AI Scribe for a Psychiatric Practice Four questions, in the order that matters. Does It Structure the MSE or Just Transcribe It Run a test visit and read the output. If the mental status exam arrives as a sentence instead of populated domains, the tool was built for a different specialty. Does It Keep the Prescriber as the Clinician of Record Ask whether the audit trail records what the AI drafted and what the prescriber changed [1]. You are signing the note. The record should make clear that the clinical judgment was yours. Does It Handle the Coding Boundary or Leave It to You Give it a visit with both an E/M component and psychotherapy. If the note comes back as one narrative, you are still doing the split by hand. Does It Write Into the EHR or Hand You Text to Paste A note you copy and paste is a note you touched twice. Ask specifically whether it writes natively into your EHR, and whether that holds for every provider in the practice. Where Sully.ai Fits for Psychiatric Prescribers Sully.ai's AI Scribe captures the visit and writes documentation into the EHR, and clinicians can save how they want their notes structured so the MSE and medication sections come back the same way every time. It runs on a single integration across Epic, Cerner, Meditech, and Athenahealth . What happens next is the part a scribe alone cannot do. The AI Coder reads the finished note, extracts the ICD-10 and CPT codes, and submits a clean claim, so the coding boundary is handled rather than handed back to you. The AI Receptionist books the follow-up interval you just dictated. Sully operates across 5,000+ providers , has delivered 50M+ hours of AI work, and prices each AI role 80 to 90 percent below the human equivalent. If you want to see it on a psychiatric workflow specifically, there is a dedicated psychiatry scribe page and a broader behavioral health overview. Book a demo and bring a real med-management visit. FAQ Q: What should an AI scribe for psychiatry do that a general medical scribe does not? It should structure the mental status exam by domain rather than summarizing it, capture medication regimens with dosages, adherence, side effects and the rationale for each change, document a risk assessment with dynamic, static, and protective factors, and support the coding split when an E/M service and psychotherapy occur in the same visit. General ambient scribes are tuned for primary care encounters and tend to flatten all four. Q: Can an AI scribe handle a medication management visit? Yes, if it is built for it. The note has to show the current regimen, dosages, adherence, perceived efficacy, side effects, prescribing rationale, refills authorized, and the follow-up interval [2]. Sully.ai's AI Scribe captures this during the visit and writes it into the EHR, and the AI Coder takes the finished note through to a submitted claim. Q: How does psychiatric coding affect documentation? A prescriber's follow-up bills an evaluation and management code, 99212 to 99215 established or 99202 to 99205 new, selected on medical decision making or total time. If psychotherapy also happened in that visit you add +90833 for 16 to 37 minutes, +90836 for 38 to 52 minutes, or +90838 for 53 minutes or more, with the psychotherapy minutes counted separately from the E/M work, which means both components have to be documented separately in the note. You cannot bill a stand-alone psychotherapy code (90832, 90834, 90837) alongside an E/M on the same date, because it denies as a duplicate service. The initial evaluation uses 90791 without medical services or 90792 with, and neither is time-based [4]. Q: Are AI scribes safe for substance use treatment records? Substance use treatment records are governed by 42 CFR Part 2, which is stricter than HIPAA [3]. Ask any vendor directly whether they support it, alongside a signed BAA and encryption of protected health information. Q: Do you have free psychiatry note templates? Yes. Sully publishes four: a psychiatry SOAP note, a psychiatric intake evaluation, a DAP note, and a behavioral health BIRP note. Each has the payer requirements built into the page, including clock times plus total time, the encounter and coding fields with place of service and telehealth modifiers, means access in the risk section, and an attestation block. title: How to Master Airbnb Inventory Management Like a Pro
summary: Fix your Airbnb inventory management before a missing toiletry costs your vacation rental a five-star review.
body_text: Your cleaning team has a checklist. Your supply closet gets restocked. Guests still message at 11pm about missing toilet paper. Here is where the process is actually breaking down. Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads think that tighter checklists and more diligent manual tracking are the solution, if the cleaning team just checks more carefully and the spreadsheet stays current, inventory problems will stop slipping through. But Airbnb inventory management is one of those operational areas where hosts feel busy and the system keeps failing them anyway. The cleaning team has a checklist. See our AI for hospitality for how this works in practice. The supply closet gets restocked. Photos document every room. And yet, a guest still messages at 11pm asking where the toilet paper is. For teams running hospitality operations at scale, that gap between "we have a process" and "the process actually works" is where reviews and revenue quietly disappear. The breakdown almost never lives in the checklist itself. It lives in what happens after the cleaner finishes and before the next guest checks in. That window is where signals die. Airbnb inventory management is the systematic process of tracking, organizing, and replenishing every item a guest needs across your rental properties so that nothing is discovered missing mid-stay. It is not a one-time stock-up before a busy season. It is an ongoing operational discipline that connects physical supply levels to the people responsible for maintaining them, on a defined schedule, every single turnover. The distinction matters because most hosts treat inventory as a purchasing problem. In practice, the failure point is rarely "we forgot to buy it." It is "we bought it, but no one confirmed it made it into the property before the guest arrived." Treating all inventory the same is where most systems break. There are three distinct categories, each demanding a different management rhythm. Consumables - Items That Deplete Every Stay Consumables include toilet paper, soap, coffee pods, garbage bags, and batteries. These items deplete with every stay, which means their failure mode is predictable and entirely preventable with the right replenishment rhythm. The challenge is not sourcing them, it is confirming they made it into the property before the guest arrived. A consumables process that ends at the supply closet, rather than at the guest-ready room, is where that 11pm message originates. Linens - Items That Wear Out Over Time Linens, towels, sheets, and pillowcases, wear out over time and require rotation, not just restock. The standard benchmark is two full sets per bed so turnovers never stall waiting on laundry. Unlike consumables, the failure mode here is slower and easier to miss. A fraying pillowcase or a thin towel does not trigger a reorder alert; it shows up in a guest review. Managing linens well means tracking condition and rotation cycles, not just counting units on a shelf. Assets - Items That Degrade Without Depleting Assets, appliances, furniture, cookware, and safety equipment, do not deplete but do degrade. Their failures show up in guest reviews, not consumables checklists, which makes them the easiest category to neglect until something goes visibly wrong. Because assets do not trigger a reorder signal the way a missing soap bar does, they require a separate inspection cadence entirely. A wobbly chair and a malfunctioning coffee maker both live outside the standard turnover checklist, and that is precisely where most asset problems quietly accumulate. Key takeaways Airbnb inventory management breaks down as a communication problem, not a counting problem, no one knows what's missing, replaced, or broken until a guest reports it at 11pm. Tighter checklists and more careful cleaners don't fix the gap between 'documented' and 'confirmed', they just move the failure point one step later in the turnover. PAR level tracking tells you when to reorder; it says nothing about whether the right item is actually on the shelf for the guests checking in this weekend. Physical storage organization, labels, bins, photo standards, is the only mechanism that makes a cleaner's report consistent and auditable without a supervisor on-site. At ten or more properties, every unresolved inventory signal sits in a human inbox waiting to be read, interpreted, and routed, that wait is where portfolios bleed time and ratings. Erwan Le Roy's 35-property operation reached 96% automation and sub-1-minute response times not by counting inventory more carefully, but by removing the human-in-the-middle from routine ops and guest touchpoints. Conduit's AI-powered guest communication platform closes that coordination gap, routing signals, responding to guests, and keeping ops moving around the clock without a human relay in between. The Real Cost of Manual Inventory Tracking Across Multiple Properties At ten properties, the gap between "we have a system" and "the system is working" becomes expensive. Most vacation rental property managers and operations leads believe that tighter checklists and more diligent manual tracking are the solution, if the cleaning team just checks more carefully and the spreadsheet stays current, inventory problems will stop slipping through. Scale that to ten, fifteen, or thirty properties and the volume of handoffs between cleaners, ops leads, and suppliers multiplies every failure point until no single person can hold the full picture. The same coordination collapse that breaks inventory tracking breaks guest communication, and the two failures compound each other when a guest messages about a missing amenity and the reply falls through the cracks. Why Manual Tracking Collapses at 10 or 30 Properties The failure mode is predictable. Each additional property adds another communication layer: a different cleaner, a different supplier contact, a different restock schedule. What worked as a shared mental model at two units becomes a game of telephone at ten. Checklists don't break because hosts stop caring; they break because the signal that something is missing has to travel through too many handoffs before anyone acts on it. Multi-property inventory management stops being a counting problem and starts being a coordination problem the moment you add your fourth or fifth unit. The same dynamic plays out in guest messaging. Operations teams managing communications across multiple platforms, Airbnb, direct booking sites, VRBO, find that the volume of incoming messages across ten or more properties makes consistent, timely replies nearly impossible without adding headcount. Conduit's Inbox is most beneficial: when your team is monitoring and managing guest conversations across multiple platforms or properties simultaneously, a single unified view replaces the context-switching that lets messages age unanswered. The operations or support team uses it on an ongoing basis to monitor, review, and manage all conversations the AI agent is handling, meaning nothing requires a human to catch it first before it gets a response. The Compounding Review Risk Inside Every Missed Restock A missing roll of toilet paper costs less than a dollar. The review it generates can cost far more. Cleanliness and missing amenities are among the most frequently mentioned categories in negative Airbnb reviews, appearing in a significant share of one- and two-star ratings. The math is asymmetric: the item is trivial, the reputational exposure is not. A single negative review on a high-performing listing can meaningfully affect booking momentum, turning a trivial supply gap into a measurable revenue event, a risk that compounds the longer the listing carries the lower rating. The review risk doesn't stop at the physical amenity. A guest who messages mid-stay about a missing item and receives no reply, or a slow, inconsistent one, is far more likely to put that frustration into a public review. Property managers we work with who are scaling past ten units describe exactly this pattern: the inventory problem is the spark, but the unanswered or delayed guest message is what turns it into a one-star rating. Conduit's AI Agents are most beneficial precisely when a business receives a high volume of repetitive guest messages and has existing documentation, SOPs, FAQs, property manuals, to train the agent on. Once connected to that documentation, the agent begins handling first automated guest replies and then responds continuously, whenever a guest sends a message, before, during, or after a stay. The result is that a mid-stay complaint about a missing amenity gets an immediate, consistent acknowledgment rather than sitting in a queue until an ops lead cycles back to that inbox. The 80/20 Reality of Inventory Pain The item is trivial, the reputational exposure is not. Toilet paper, hand soap, paper towels, coffee supplies, and dish soap follow an 80/20 pattern: a small group of high-velocity consumables drives the bulk of mid-stay complaints and emergency restock runs. These are also the items hosts most under-systematize, because they feel too simple to formalize. Formalizing PAR levels (minimum stock thresholds) for these items is the operational lever, but it only holds if the communication layer around it also scales. That communication layer is where most growing portfolios leak. Adding a fifteenth property should not require a fifteenth communication queue. Conduit's Workflows are most beneficial when a business has recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action, exactly the restock-reminder, check-in confirmation, and post-stay follow-up sequences that pile up as a portfolio grows. Workflows fire after a trigger event in a conversation or guest lifecycle: after a booking is confirmed, after check-in, or when a specific keyword is detected. Pair that with Integrations that let the AI agent pull from tools your team already uses, Notion, Google Drive, Airbnb, without manual re-entry, and the coordination overhead of each new property shrinks instead of compounding. The promise is straightforward: add properties without adding coordination headcount, and reduce the time spent on the manual, repetitive messaging tasks that currently fill the gap between a guest complaint and a resolved one. How to Build Your Airbnb Inventory Checklist - Room by Room, Category by Category The checklist sitting in your property's Google Drive is not the problem. The problem is that a checklist documents what should be there, not what actually is there the moment a guest pulls back the shower curtain at 9pm. That gap between "documented" and "confirmed" is where bad reviews are born, and where a systemized, scalable operation separates itself from one that depends entirely on the owner catching every problem personally. 1. Bedroom Linen Inventory - Track Every Sheet Set, Pillow, and Duvet by Room Two complete sets of sheets and pillowcases per bed is the industry baseline for short-term rentals, with a third set recommended for properties running same-day turnovers. Track each set by room, not by property total. A property total tells you nothing about whether the right linen is on the right bed right now. A bedroom checklist card pinned inside the linen closet, photographed by the cleaner on every turnover, gives you a timestamped confirmation that the right set is on the right bed. Without that photo, the checklist is a wish list. Conduit.ai's Integrations pull that content directly so your AI agent can reference current room-level linen standards without manual re-entry, keeping your turnover communication consistent across every property without owner involvement on each check. 2. Bathroom Consumables Inventory - Toiletries, Towels, and Replenishment Thresholds Missing or insufficient supplies are among the most frequently cited reasons guests leave negative Airbnb reviews, and the bathroom is ground zero. Stock toilet paper, hand soap, shampoo, body wash, and a spare roll minimum per bathroom. Two bath towels and one hand towel per guest covers the standard stay. Consumables deplete invisibly between turnover photos, so a threshold-based reorder trigger matters more here than anywhere else on your vacation rental essentials list. One pattern worth noting: hosts who feel pressure to over-communicate every item to guests often end up with checkout instructions that run to four pages or more. Guests find that overwhelming, and it signals a host who hasn't separated operational inventory tracking (your internal system) from guest-facing communication (what guests actually need to know). Keep your consumable thresholds in your internal SOPs; keep guest instructions to what is genuinely reasonable and actionable. Conduit.ai's AI Agents, trained on those internal SOPs and FAQs, handle the guest-facing side, answering supply questions before, during, and after a stay, so the operational detail stays where it belongs and guests never see a four-page wall of requirements. 3. Kitchen Equipment Checklist - Appliances, Cookware, and Utensils by Function Organize kitchen inventory by function: prep (cutting boards, knives, mixing bowls), cook (pots, pans, baking sheet), and serve (plates, glasses, utensils for guest count plus two). Appliances including the coffee maker, toaster, and microwave deserve their own line items with condition notes, not just a checkmark. In our experience managing active rental properties, appliance replacement is a recurring annual cost, which means your kitchen inventory list needs a separate replacement-budget column, not just a present/absent field. When a guest messages at 9pm asking why the coffee maker isn't working, that question is repetitive, predictable, and expensive to handle manually across multiple properties. Conduit.ai's AI Agents are most beneficial exactly here, high-volume, repetitive guest messages that your existing documentation can answer, so your operations team monitors outcomes rather than fielding every individual message. 4. Living Room and Common Area Inventory - Furniture, Entertainment, and Comfort Items Living room inventory is often under-documented because items feel permanent, yet throw blankets, remote controls, board games, and charging cables disappear regularly. A room-by-room checklist should include serial numbers for electronics and condition notes for upholstered furniture. This category matters most for hosts competing on 'home-like feel' rather than price. The tradeoff: logging every small comfort item is time-intensive but prevents the slow inventory bleed that degrades guest experience over months. 5. Outdoor and Patio Inventory - Furniture, Grills, and Seasonal Equipment Outdoor inventory is the most frequently under-documented category on a room-by-room checklist. Patio furniture, grills, and seasonal items are exposed to weather and, in some markets, have meaningful theft and damage rates that make condition tracking essential. Log each piece by item, condition, and last-inspection date. Grill accessories (brush, propane level, cover) deserve their own sub-list. Properties that skip outdoor documentation consistently discover damage through guest complaints rather than turnover checks. A scalable operation does not rely on the owner remembering to ask about the patio after every turnover. Conduit.ai's Workflows trigger automatically after booking confirmation or check-in. Recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require manual staff action are exactly where Workflows add the most value, so the right follow-up happens whether the owner is watching or not. 6. Cleaning Supplies Inventory - Turnover Kits, Restocking Carts, and Cleaner Access Standardize your turnover kit at the property level, not the cleaner level. When the kit is defined in your SOPs, quantities, product names, storage location, and those SOPs live in a connected system, every cleaner and every automated workflow pulls from the same source of truth. Conduit.ai's Integrations are built for exactly this: if your cleaning SOPs already exist in Google Drive or Notion, your AI agent leverages that content directly without manual re-entry, so your turnover standards scale to every additional property without scaling your personal involvement alongside them. 7. Guest Welcome and Safety Inventory - Starter Packs, Emergency Items, and House Manuals Welcome and safety inventory covers the items guests notice first and remember longest: a starter toiletry pack, first-aid kit, fire extinguisher, flashlight, and a printed or digital house manual. For mid-term stays of one to two months, hosts must decide between a minimal starter pack and a fully stocked approach, a decision that directly affects both cost and review scores. The key limitation: safety items like smoke detectors and extinguishers require compliance-driven inspection schedules, not just inventory counts. PAR Level Tracking - How to Set Reorder Points Before You Run Out PAR levels are genuinely useful, but they only address half of what makes short-term rental inventory management break down. Setting a reorder threshold tells you when to act; it says nothing about whether the item sitting on the shelf right now is the right item, in the right quantity, for the guests checking in this weekend. A property running on PAR levels alone can hit every restock trigger perfectly and still send a family of five into a unit stocked for two, or leave a cleaning crew short on supplies because the threshold was set against average turnover, not a back-to-back booking weekend. Reactive restocking has a hidden failure rate most operators never measure: by the time a cleaner notices the toilet paper is low, there is often only one stay left before a guest finds none. That gap between observation and action is where stockouts live, and no amount of careful eyeballing closes it across a growing portfolio, especially when you are running a lean team or managing multiple properties solo. Every hour spent chasing a restock is an hour not spent protecting the review scores that keep your calendar full. PAR Levels Defined - The Minimum Quantity That Triggers a Reorder Signal, Not a Reminder PAR level tracking means assigning a specific minimum quantity to each stocked item so the reorder signal fires at a threshold, not when someone happens to notice. For consumables, that threshold is calculated from actual consumption data, not intuition. A host running a four-guest cabin stay of three to four nights needs at least four rolls of toilet paper per bathroom to cover the stay comfortably. Operators who set PAR levels from actual consumption data, tracking how many rolls a four-guest, three-night stay uses rather than defaulting to flat rules, consistently report fewer mid-stay complaints and less emergency restocking than those relying on intuition. The principle is straightforward: a threshold grounded in real usage eliminates the gap between "we stocked it" and "the guest had enough." The PAR level is not a counting exercise; it is a communication protocol that removes the human memory trigger from every routine restock decision. Conduit's AI Agents and Workflows earn their place in an operations stack. Because Workflows fire after trigger events in the guest lifecycle, after a booking is confirmed, after check-in, or when a specific keyword is detected, an operator can build a trigger that flags a potential inventory shortfall the moment a longer-than-average stay books, prompting the right action before the cleaner ever sets foot in the unit. Critically, the operator or ops lead sets those rules; no IT department is required. A solo host or lean team can configure the logic once and let it run continuously, protecting review scores by surfacing issues fast enough to resolve them before a guest ever notices. A correctly set PAR level with no verified reset mechanism produces the same failure mode as no PAR level at all, because cleaner accountability for inventory is assumed rather than formally assigned, many cleaners bundle it into turnover implicitly without documentation, meaning the threshold exists on paper but is never reliably checked. Conduit's Inbox consolidates guest and operations communications across multiple platforms and properties simultaneously, so when a cleaner flags a low-stock item mid-turnover, that message surfaces in one monitored place rather than getting lost across a fragmented thread of texts and channel messages. The AI Agent handles the high-volume, repetitive confirmations, restocking acknowledgments, supply request replies, while the operations team reviews the conversations that actually need human judgment, keeping a lean team genuinely lean. How to Set PAR Levels for the Three Inventory Categories - Consumables, Linens, and Assets The formula differs by category. For consumables, multiply average nightly usage by your longest typical stay, then add a 20 percent buffer. For linens, the hospitality industry benchmark is a minimum of two complete sets per bed, one in use, one clean for a same-day turnover without an emergency laundry run. For assets (coffee makers, hair dryers, extra blankets), PAR is simpler: one working unit per designated use point. Conduit's Integrations: the AI Agent can draw on that existing content directly, without manual re-entry, so the PAR logic you have already written becomes the knowledge base the agent uses to answer supply questions from cleaners, co-hosts, or guests, the moment a message arrives, before, during, or after a stay. How to Organize Airbnb Inventory Storage - Labels, Bins, and a Dedicated Housekeeping Area Think of your housekeeping closet as a piece of software. The labels are the interface. The bins are the logic. The photo standard is the documentation. When any one of those three is missing, the cleaner is left writing their own code on every turnover, and the output is unpredictable. It is the only reliable mechanism for making a shortage visible to a cleaner in under 60 seconds without a supervisor present. When absence is visually obvious rather than discovered through counting, shortage detection moves from your inbox to the cleaner's eyes at the moment it can still be fixed. The physical system and the digital layer reinforce each other. Conduit's Integrations pull existing content into active operations without manual re-entry. The housekeeping closet becomes the physical node; the integrated workspace becomes the operational backbone behind it. 1. Color-Coded Bin System - Zone Every Supply Category by Room Color-coded bins assign a dedicated color to each supply zone (bathroom, kitchen, bedroom, laundry) so a cleaner scanning the shelf knows immediately which category is low without reading a single label. The visual signal works faster than a checklist because it removes interpretation. The real tradeoff: initial bin standardization costs time upfront, and multi-property operations must commit to the same color scheme at every unit or the system creates confusion rather than clarity. For operators managing guest communications across multiple properties simultaneously, the bin system also reduces the volume of mid-turnover messages that end up in the host's inbox. When the shortage is visible at the shelf, the cleaner resolves it on the spot, and a message that was never sent is a thread that never needs monitoring. Conduit's Inbox is designed for exactly the conversations that do make it through: ongoing monitoring, review, and management of all AI-handled guest threads, most valuable when communications are flowing across multiple platforms or properties at once. 2. Property-Specific Linen Labeling - Iron-On Tags to Prevent Cross-Property Mix-Ups Iron-on or sewn-in tags with a property code ensure linens that leave in a laundry bag return to the right unit. Linen and supply mis-routing is a recurring operational error for operators managing three or more units, making property-coded tags one of the higher-leverage, lower-cost interventions available to growing portfolios. This method is most valuable when your cleaning team services multiple properties in a single day; for a single-property host, the overhead of tagging rarely justifies the effort. The same logic that makes property coding valuable in the closet applies to guest communication: when messages arrive from multiple properties across platforms, without a system they blur together. Conduit's AI Agents are most beneficial when a business receives a high volume of repetitive guest messages and has existing documentation, SOPs, FAQs, and supply manuals to train the agent on. Connecting those documents through a tool like Notion or Google Drive means the agent can reference property-specific context rather than returning generic answers, the digital equivalent of the iron-on tag. 3. Dedicated Housekeeping Closet with Printed Zone Signs - Hotel-Style Organization at Home Designating a single locked closet exclusively for housekeeping supplies, stocked with printed zone signs for 'Cleaning Chemicals,' 'Guest Amenities,' and 'Spare Linens', mirrors hotel back-of-house efficiency. This setup dramatically cuts turnover time because cleaners never hunt for supplies. The tradeoff is space: smaller properties or studio rentals may lack a dedicated closet, requiring a rolling cart alternative instead. 4. Par-Level Stocking Method - Set Minimum Quantities Per Bin to Trigger Automatic Reorders Write the minimum acceptable quantity directly on each bin with a permanent marker or printed label. When the bin visually falls to or below that line, the reorder signal is immediate and requires no counting, no memory, and no supervisor. The par level is the threshold; the label is the alert mechanism. Conduit's Integrations layer allows the AI agent handling guest and operational messages to reference current supply standards without a staff member manually relaying the information. This is most beneficial when the business already uses those tools and wants the AI agent to leverage existing content without manual re-entry. The par label on the bin and the SOP in the shared drive become two expressions of the same standard: one physical, one digital, both reducing the moment a shortage becomes someone else's problem to solve from scratch. 5. Turnover-Ready Supply Caddy - Pre-Packed Per-Checkout Kit for Cleaners A pre-packed caddy assembled after each checkout, containing exactly the right quantities of cleaning sprays, microfiber cloths, and guest amenity restocks for one full turnover, means cleaners arrive and start immediately with zero prep time. Best for high-frequency hosts with back-to-back bookings. The tradeoff is that caddy assembly requires a reliable post-checkout inventory check, adding a step that's easy to skip under time pressure. How to Integrate Inventory Checking Into Your Cleaning Team Turnover Workflow The cleaner has already left. The host is twenty minutes away. The next guest checks in at 4pm. This is the exact window where inventory gaps become guest complaints, and it closes faster than any manual verification process can move. Make the Cleaner's Sign-Off Do Double Duty - Clean Property and Confirmed Stock Levels Integrating inventory verification into the cleaning team turnover workflow is the most reliable way to close that window. Assign the cleaner's sign-off as a two-part confirmation, where marking a property "ready" requires both a clean-space check and a stock-level check in the same step. The two tasks share the same physical moment, the same person, and the same location, so bundling them costs almost no additional time. The core argument here is worth stating directly: the inventory accountability gap is not caused by negligent cleaners; it is caused by structural role ambiguity that no checklist alone can resolve. Because inventory responsibility gets bundled into turnover implicitly , cleaners operate under an assumed scope the host never confirmed, and hosts operate under an assumed verification the cleaner never performed. This is not a hypothetical edge case. A recurring concern among short-term rental operators is that inventory and move-out inspection checklists get processed without independent verification, leaving both guests and cleaners in a position where the record of what was checked, and by whom, is disputed after the fact. Adding checklist line items into that ambiguous handoff doesn't fix the gap; it adds compliance surface area to a role boundary that was never drawn. The fix is a non-optional, role-explicit verification trigger embedded in the workflow itself, making the inventory check a discrete, confirmed event rather than an implied byproduct of showing up. What makes this structurally difficult to solve at scale is the same thing that makes guest communication difficult to solve at scale: volume compounds faster than headcount can absorb it. Jack, CEO of Haven Vacation Rentals, described the inflection point clearly after his team began systematically closing operational gaps: "We added 14 listings in January." That kind of growth-without-proportional-overhead only becomes possible when recurring, predictable touchpoints, including turnover verification, stop requiring a dedicated human decision at every step. The inventory check is exactly that kind of touchpoint: predictable, recurring, and currently eating labor it doesn't need to. The same dynamic shows up on the guest communication side. At 270 properties, Haven's support model required roughly 25 staff across multiple shifts to handle check-in questions, lockouts, cleaning issues, and complaints. Before workflows and a properly trained knowledge base were in place, even a partial automation layer wasn't enough to change how the team operated; growth still meant more messages, more calls, and more hiring. Once the operational structure caught up, the difference was measurable. Jack's own account of a Sunday morning check captures it: "I remember looking at my phone, and I'm like, how in the world am I gonna look at all 100 of these problems? Then on Sunday, I looked, and there was three things. And I was like, oh, this is great." That reduction didn't come from working harder; it came from building workflows that handled the predictable before it became a problem. Inventory verification sits in exactly that category. Assign Inventory Zones by Role, Not by Memory - Who Checks What and When A zone-based assignment removes the ambiguity. Divide the property into discrete areas (bathroom, kitchen, bedroom, utility closet) and assign each zone to a named role with a named trigger. No zone is "done" until its stock confirmation is logged, not just its cleaning tasks. When a guest messages about missing toiletries, the zone log shows exactly which check was completed and when, protecting the cleaner from unfair blame and giving the ops lead a specific failure point to address. This structure also directly addresses a legitimate concern operators face when disputes arise: without an independently verified, timestamped record of what was checked and by whom, inventory claims become a matter of competing accounts rather than documented fact. A zone-based log with role-explicit sign-offs creates the kind of paper trail that resolves those disputes quickly, and discourages them from forming in the first place. How to Use Turno to Embed Inventory Checks Into Every Turnover Task Flow Turno (formerly TurnoverBnB) supports this structure directly through its task template builder. Each cleaning step carries a companion inventory checkbox immediately below it; the cleaner cannot mark the property ready without confirming stock levels in each zone. That confirmation becomes a timestamped record tied to a named role, not a memory, not an assumption, and not an implied byproduct of the turnover visit. Conduit connects to this at the guest communication layer downstream. When a guest checks in and messages about a missing item, the AI agent, trained on your SOPs, property manuals, and turnover protocols, can cross-reference the zone log context surfaced through your integrations (Google Drive, Notion, or your property management system) and respond immediately, before the question reaches a human queue. Conduit's Workflows trigger on specific keywords or guest lifecycle events, including the check-in window, so a guest message about missing toiletries doesn't sit unanswered while your ops lead is between properties. The agent handles the first response, routes the exception if it needs human action, and logs the interaction in the unified Inbox where your team monitors all active conversations across every platform and property simultaneously. The inventory verification workflow and the guest communication workflow become a single closed loop: the turnover confirms the stock, the AI agent handles the guest if something was missed, and your team sees only the exceptions that genuinely require them. The software detects the gap; a person reads the alert, messages the cleaner, confirms the restock, and updates the guest if check-in is affected. At three properties, that chain is manageable. At fifteen, it is a part-time job nobody officially owns. That bottleneck is sharpest for hosts who started out tracking linens, supplies, and bookings in Excel or iCal. iCal syncs dates but carries zero inventory state. It cannot record that you have five units of one room type running low on towels and ten of another running fine. When the tracking layer is a spreadsheet and the alert layer is a mental note, unexpected stockouts become a recurring cost of doing business rather than an edge case. Hosts scaling past their first few properties feel this most acutely: the manual touchpoints that were manageable at two units compound into a fragmented ops burden at ten. AI Workflows fire after the trigger event occurs rather than waiting for a staff member to open their inbox. Turno - Best for Cleaner-Linked Supply Tracking and Low-Stock Alerts Turno embeds inventory checks directly into the post-turnover workflow, so low-stock flags fire as a byproduct of the clean rather than a separate manual audit. Cleaners log supply levels during the turnover; the platform alerts the host automatically when an item drops below threshold. The tradeoff: Turno's strength is the cleaner-to-host signal chain, not downstream ops routing. Once the alert lands, a human still owns the follow-through, and for multi-property operators fielding those alerts across several inboxes simultaneously, pairing Turno's detection layer with an automated communication layer is where the time savings compound. 3. Breezeway - Best for Operations-Level Inventory Auditing Across Large Portfolios Breezeway embeds property condition and supply checks into structured inspection workflows, making it a strong fit for portfolios above 20 units where ad-hoc auditing collapses under volume. Operators who implement structured inspection workflows, the model Breezeway's platform is built around, generally report cleaner audit trails and fewer ambiguous post-checkout disputes than those relying on unstructured cleaner notes, a pattern consistent with how formalized verification reduces gap-in-memory conflicts. Ops leads get a consistent audit trail across every property, not just the ones a cleaner happened to flag. The limitation is setup overhead: standardizing inspection templates across a large portfolio takes real configuration time before the system pays back. 4. Hostaway - Best for PMS-Native Inventory Visibility Tied to Booking Data Hostaway surfaces inventory flags inside the same dashboard that manages bookings and channel distribution, so high-occupancy windows can trigger restock prompts automatically based on booking density rather than a cleaner's manual note. For teams already managing guest communications across multiple platforms, connecting Hostaway's booking signals to an AI tool means the downstream guest communication, the check-in update, the delay notice, the confirmation message, can be handled by an AI agent pulling from the same SOPs the ops team already maintains, without manual re-entry. The tradeoff: PMS-native inventory features cover the basics well but lack the granular audit trails a dedicated ops platform provides. 5. WaspBarcode - Best for Barcode-Scanned Physical Asset Tracking in Vacation Rentals WaspBarcode applies warehouse-grade barcode scanning to physical asset tracking, making it the strongest fit for operators who need to account for durable goods, furniture, appliances, equipment, across multiple properties rather than consumable supplies alone. Why Inventory Management at Scale Is Really a Communication Problem: and How AI Agents Solve It Every tool in your inventory stack, from the PAR-level spreadsheet to the low-stock alert in your PMS, was built to solve a detection problem. And at scale, every low-stock alert, every Turno flag, every Breezeway inspection still terminates at a human inbox where latency lives.
